profiles.intent: Enantioselective synthesis using small organic catalysts, including chiral peptides and noncovalent organocatalysts.

pool.title: Photocatalytic tetrapeptides for enantioselective visible light-induced transformations
pool.abstract: Abstract Research on enantioselective photocatalysis has so far been focused on molecular photocatalysts or large yet easily adaptable photoenzymes. However, both catalysis classes display deficiencies either due to their limited adaptability or their high molecular weight. Here we show that small peptides can bridge the gap between the currently used photocatalysts by combining structural flexibility and low molecular weight. We constructed a small peptide that displays a pyroglutamic acid at its N terminus for substrate recognition. At the C terminus, a thioxanthone-based amino acid was installed to harvest photons and to act catalytically by energy transfer. Two amino acids were sufficient to link the two components, resulting in a photocatalytically active tetrapeptide that was used both for photochemical deracemization and enantioselective [2 + 2] photocycloaddition reactions. Our results demonstrate that small peptides with a molecular weight below 750 Da can act as efficient molecular catalysts for enantioselective photochemical transformations.
pool.authors: Robert M. Irle, Irene Lazzarini, Franz Hagn, Martin Zacharias, Thorsten Bach

pool.title: Two‐Phase Electrochemical Vicinal Dibromination of Alkenes With Sodium Bromide as the Bromine Source and Supporting Electrolyte
pool.abstract: An environmentally friendly two‐phase electrochemical method for the vicinal dibromination of alkenes has been developed. This strategy utilizes inexpensive sodium bromide as both the bromine source and the supporting electrolyte without the use of catalysts, external oxidants, and strong acids. It features simple operation, mild reaction conditions, broad substrate scope, and high efficiency, affording the desired products in up to 97% yield.
pool.authors: Xiaolong Wang, Xuege Su, 凌杰 陈, Qian He

pool.title: Recent Advances in Boryl Radical Chemistry: The Rise of Visible‐Light‐Mediated Lewis Base‐Coordinated Borane Chemistry
pool.abstract: Comprehensive Summary Lewis base‐coordinated borane is air‐stable, easy to handle, and employed as a boryl radical precursor under both thermal and photochemical conditions. Over the past few decades, the traditional ionic hydroboration method has been complemented by significant developments in radical‐based hydroboration protocols, enabling the synthesis of diverse, value‐added organoboron compounds. In this review, we have endeavored to present the state of the art in visible‐light‐driven Lewis base‐coordinated boryl radical‐promoted hydroboration, borylation, and XAT (X = halogen, H, CN) reactions, with a discussion covering reaction types, mechanisms, trends, and the distinctions between photo‐induced and thermal‐induced processes. The review presents a comprehensive overview of this theme, which has sparked significant research interest. Key Scientists
pool.authors: Yuqi Miao, Xuenian Chen

pool.title: Synthesis of Carbon Quantum Dots (CQDs) and their applications as catalyst in organic synthesis: A comprehensive review
pool.abstract: Carbon Quantum Dots (CQDs) are an advancing class of carbon- based nanomaterials with dimensions usually around 10 nm which display remarkable properties such as minimal toxicity, high chemical stability, good aqueous solubility, notable biocompatibility and strong tuneable photoluminescence. CQDs exhibit broad range of applications such as photocatalysis, ion sensing, biological imaging, heavy metal detection, super capacitor, membrane fabrication and water pollution treatment. This review brings forth a broad summary of the various synthetic strategies for CQDs and the role of CQDs as catalysts in various organic synthesis have also been included. In wake of the unique electronic and surface chemistry CQDs demonstrate superior performance in various organic reactions, such as condensation, oxidation, reduction, coupling, and cyclization. At the outset, we discuss the existing constraints and potential research directions in the field which furnish comprehensive insights into the growing potential of CQDs as sustainable and efficient catalysts in modern organic synthesis.
pool.authors: Quamrin N. Shaikh, Rahul R. Mahire

pool.title: CAN-Promoted Boc2O-Mediated Cascade Conversion of Aziridines to Oxazolidinones
pool.abstract: Abstract An efficient CAN-promoted Boc2O-mediated cascade conversion of aziridines to oxazolidinones has been developed. The transformation proceeds under mild, CO2-free conditions and provides structurally diverse oxazolidinones in 16–99% yields (46 examples), with gram-scale reactions demonstrating its synthetic practicality. Boc2O serves as an alternative carbonyl source and is proposed to generate a reactive tert-butyl carbonate species that undergoes nucleophilic aziridine ring opening followed by intramolecular cyclization. Control experiments identify CAN as the most effective promoter examined and demonstrate that DBU and TBAB cooperatively enhance reaction efficiency. Stereochemical studies are consistent with an SN2-type ring-opening pathway. This methodology provides a practical complement to existing CO2-based approaches and expands the synthetic utility of Boc2O-mediated cascade chemistry.
pool.authors: Yujin Huang, Meng‐Hsia Tsai, Xin-Ni Zhan, Po-Wei Wu, Cheng‐Kun Lin

pool.title: FtmOx1-catalyzed diverse C(sp3)-H oxyfunctionalization enables versatile late-stage diversification of phenethylamines and tetrahydroisoquinolines
pool.abstract: The enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp3)-H bonds has emerged as a transformative strategy in medicinal chemistry. Verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is known to catalyze the endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, we demonstrate the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 by showing its ability to mediate diverse C(sp3)-H transformations on non-native substrates—phenethylamine and tetrahydroisoquinoline derivatives (1) —including β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α,β-desaturation. A total of 48 structurally diverse substrates prove suitable for this method, substantially expanding the biocatalytic repertoire of FtmOx1. Mechanistic studies, combined with crystallographic and mutagenesis analyses, reveal the distinct molecular basis for this diverse C(sp3)-H oxyfunctionalization compared to native pathway. Notably, the relative flexibility of the phenethyl and benzyl chains of 1, assisted by specific substitutions that allow the two chains to swing, enables high β-selectivity for hydroxylation and prevents secondary oxidation. This C(sp3)-H activation platform efficiently generates structurally diverse oxyfunctionalized derivatives, including 1,2-amino alcohols (2), 1,2-amino ketones (3), and enamines (4), accelerating lead discovery for modulators of the human relaxin family peptide receptor 4 (RXFP4). Collectively, our work establishes FtmOx1 as a powerful biocatalytic tool, expanding the frontiers of C–H functionalization in drug discovery. Enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp3)-H bonds is an important strategy in medicinal chemistry, and verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is an enzyme that catalyses endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, the authors report the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 in mediating diverse C(sp3)-H transformations of non-native substrates, including phenethylamines and tetrahydroisoquinolines, through β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α, β-desaturation.
pool.authors: Jiapeng Zhang, Hengrui Liang, Aolong Shang, Chengkai Wu, Jianchang Yu, Ganlu Zhang, Yan Chen, Ming‐Wei Wang, Gong‐Li Tang, Aiai Sun, Shengbin Zhou, Hong Shu Liu

pool.title: P450-catalyzed enantiodivergent kinetic oxidation to access chiral haloalcohols
pool.abstract: Chiral recognition constitutes the central element of asymmetric catalysis. The control over stereoselectivity becomes more precise with the greater diversity of substituent groups introduced. Distinguishing between high similarity substituents has been a challenge in asymmetric catalysis. Herein, we report an enzymatic approach enabling kinetically enantioselective hydroxylation of (2-chloropropyl)benzene derivatives with excellent stereoselectivity, though the difference of substituent radius between methyl and chloro substituents is 0.07 Å. The cytochrome P450 enzyme P450PL2 is engineered through multiple mutagenesis strategies to enhance both its substrate selectivity and stereoselectivity, thereby enabling the enantiodivergent synthesis of haloalcohols with two stereocenters. Molecular dynamic simulations and DFT calculations infer that the engineered P450PL2 exhibits steric discrimination capability, which enables host-guest interaction with a chiral center bearing methyl and chloro substituents. The biocatalytic system provides efficient access to the 2-chloro-benzyl alcohol derivatives with up to 99:1 enantiomeric ratio and >99:1 diastereomeric ratio. Differentiation between highly similar substituents is a challenge in asymmetric catalysis. Here, the authors report an enzymatic approach enabling kinetically enantioselective hydroxylation of (2- chloropropyl)benzene derivatives using engineered P450PL2 to obtain the 2-chloro-benzyl alcohol derivatives with up to 99:1 enantiomeric ratio and >99:1 diastereomeric ratio.
pool.authors: Ting Ma, Haibo Cui, Xu Zhang, Dan Liu, Yuli Yang, Xue-Qin Ran, Hua Wan, Zheng-Yi Tang, Jie Yang, Ya Lv, Yong‐Zheng Chen

pool.title: Carbon Quaternization at the α-Position of Thiazoles: Iron-Catalyzed Hydroheteroarylation Using Unactivated Alkenes
pool.abstract: Abstract Thiazoles are privileged N-heterocyclic scaffolds ubiquitous in FDA-approved drugs, yet their clinical utility can be compromised by oxidative metabolism at the heterobenzylic position. Inspired by the metabolic-blocking strategy used in dabrafenib development, herein we report an iron-catalyzed strategy for direct α-quaternization of (benzo)thiazoles using unactivated alkenes. Under the proposed pathway, alkene-derived carbon-centered radicals undergo regioselective C2 addition and oxidative rearomatization, providing α-quaternary products without heteroarene preactivation or stoichiometric Lewis acids, thereby enabling analogue diversification.
pool.authors: Jinwoo Lee, Chaeryn Jeong, Hyungwoo Choi, Seok Beom Lee, Joonseok Jang, Sangmyung Han, Yohan Park, Suckchang Hong

pool.title: Bioinspired Heme and NonHeme Metal Complexes as Electrocatalysts for Nitrate and Nitrite Reduction
pool.abstract: Excess nitrate (NO 3 − ) and nitrite (NO 2 − ) from agricultural and industrial sources are major water pollutants and precursors of greenhouse gases. The electrocatalytic reduction of NO 3 − /NO 2 − is regarded as a sustainable solution for the remediation of contaminated water and a method for producing ammonia (NH 3 ) under ambient conditions. In this review, molecular electrocatalyst macrocycles derived from heme, such as porphyrins and phthalocyanines, and nonheme complexes for NO 3 − /NO 2 − reduction are presented. Based on enzymes such as molybdenum‐dependent nitrate reductases and copper‐ or heme‐containing nitrite reductases, representative synthetic enzymes are discussed in terms of their mechanisms, catalytic parameters, ligand effects, product selectivity, and stability. The conversion of NO 2 − to NH 3 is the most prominent application of heme‐type Fe and Co macrocycles Nonheme systems, such as Cu polypyridines, Ni diamine, or Fe/Co N‐donor complexes, can also produce NO, N 2 O, or NH 3 by varying the ligand environment or pH. We identified some advances, such as high turnover frequencies, elucidation of the competitive proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET) and atom transfer pathways, and new strategies for increased durability. Finally, the principles of second‐sphere proton relay and electronic tuning are discussed, and the opportunities for embedding macrocycles within conductive frameworks and emulating multisite enzymatic architectures to create efficient and robust electrocatalysts for nitrogen oxide (NO x ) remediation and green NH 3 production are outlined.
pool.authors: Neekita Dutta, Anukampita Borah, Satyawati deka, Biplob Borah, Sachidulal Biswas

pool.title: Post‐Oxidation Integrating Assembly‐Confined Pyrolysis to Boost POD‐Like Activity of Non‐Metal Nanozyme and Engineer Colorimetric Hydrogel for On‐Site Detection of PFAS
pool.abstract: Abstract Nanozymes have become attractive candidates for advanced sensors, yet enhancing peroxidase (POD)‐like activity of non‐metal nanozymes with minimized oxidase activity interference and broad‐spectrum recognition capability for per‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) remains challenging. Herein, we developed a “post‐oxidation integrating assembly‐confined pyrolysis” methodology for constructing high‐activity and exclusive POD‐like B, N co‐doped carbon nanozymes. Glucose and boronic acid‐involved assembly‐confined pyrolysis drove the formation of flake‐like intermediate template containing B─C bond, endowing the resultant nanozymes with well‐defined two‐dimensional (2D) morphology and abundant active sites. Interestingly, ammonium persulphate oxidation enabled POD‐like activity with at least 155.48% times and at most 310.15% times higher than controls via improving ─C═O content, sp 2 ‐C crystal domain and N doping level. Thus, a colorimetric hydrogel sensor was constructed by embedding 2D‐BN@C‐0.90 (highest activity) into polyvinyl alcohol and agarose to deliver on‐site PFAS information through an image processing algorithm, featuring low cost, ease of operation, and portability. The results demonstrated that PFASs‐bearing ─SO 3 H showed the highest inhibition efficiency, followed by ─COOH‐containing PFASs, whereas PFASs with ─OH produced the lowest one. The developed methodology promotes the scalable creation of high‐activity non‐metal nanozymes, and the as‐constructed hydrogel can tender accurate PFAS information, advancing environmental monitoring and food safety.
pool.authors: Haiyin Li, Xuan Wang, Yifan Gao, Xintong Ma, Ming Su, Zhenguo Chi, 沈益忠, Jianling Chen

pool.title: Effect of Pendant Pyrene Groups on the Topology and Thermal Properties of Poly(Trimethylene Carbonate)
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT Planar aromatic side chains offer a promising strategy for regulating polymer topology and segmental dynamics. Here, a pyrene‐substituted trimethylene carbonate (TMCM‐Py) was synthesized and polymerized by DBU‐catalyzed ring‐opening polymerization using benzyl alcohol as an initiator. Its polymerization behavior and properties were compared with those of related monomers bearing biphenyl (Bp), triphenyl (Tr), or dibenzyl (DBp) substituents. The resulting polymers exhibited apparent number‐average molecular weights of 2.3–10.8 × 10 3 with dispersities (Đ) of 1.16–1.36. MALDI‐TOF MS revealed both linear and cyclic species for polymers bearing bulky aromatic substituents, whereas cyclic species in PTMCM‐Py remained below the detection limit, qualitatively suggesting preferential linear chain propagation over backbiting‐induced cyclization. Thermogravimetric analysis showed comparable thermal stability across the series, while the glass‐transition temperature strongly depended on the side‐chain structure and reached 87°C for PTMCM‐Py. Fluorescence spectroscopy of PTMCM‐Py in dilute dichloromethane solution revealed pronounced excimer emission, indicating strong pyrene–pyrene association. Collectively, these results suggest that planar pyrene side chains promote π–π stacking networks that act as physical crosslinks, suppress backbiting, restrict segmental mobility, and substantially increase the glass‐transition temperature.
pool.authors: Ren Kojima, Julien Monot, Blanca M. Martín-Vaca, Didier Bourissou, Hiroharu Ajiro

pool.title: Alpha-Oxygenation of Ketones Using TEMPO Disproportionation
pool.abstract: Abstract The alpha-oxygenation of ketones via acid-driven TEMPO disproportionation is reported. This straightforward and robust protocol from simple starting materials exhibits an excellent substrate scope in terms of scaffold substitutions, selectivity, and functional group tolerance, with substrate limitations elucidated and highlighted. Furthermore, the mechanism was probed by way of UV–visible spectroscopy, deuterium scrambling experiments, kinetic isotope effect, and Hammett analysis to illustrate the reaction dynamics.
pool.authors: Madison A. Chupela, Jeremy M. Williamson, Brett N. Hemric

pool.title: Asymmetric Tellurium-Bonding Catalysis for Mannich Reaction.
pool.abstract: Chalcogen-bonding catalysis has recently emerged as a powerful tool in organocatalysis. Nevertheless, its application in asymmetric transformations remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the scarcity of efficient chiral chalcogen-bond donors. In this study, we report the design and synthesis of a series of chiral tellurium-bonding catalysts based on an axially chiral 1,1'-spirobiindane scaffold. Taking advantage of the highly directional and strongly polarizable tellurium-centered donors along with a well-defined C2-symmetric chiral environment, these catalysts enable cooperative bifunctional activation of substrates. Under optimized conditions, the asymmetric Mannich reaction of isatin imines with dicyanoolefins proceeds smoothly to afford a broad range of products in good to excellent yields with high enantioselectivities. Mechanistic studies support a dual chalcogen-bonding activation mode involving cooperative interactions between the two tellurium centers and the isatin imine substrate. This work constitutes a seminal contribution to asymmetric catalysis enabled by chalcogen bonding and offers a new platform for the development of chiral tellurium-bonding catalysts and related enantioselective transformations.
pool.authors: Zuo LZ, Jiang F, Lei CN, He SJ, Xiang SH, Tan B

pool.title: N‐Heterocyclic Carbene‐Triarylamine Hybrids as Redox‐Tunable Organophotocatalysts for Radical Cross‐Coupling Reactions
pool.abstract: Visible-light-induced photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful platform for organic radical transformations under mild conditions. In this field, the development of efficient photocatalysts plays a crucial role. Conventional ruthenium and iridium polypyridyl photocatalysts are limited by the expense of these precious metals. From a sustainable perspective, organic photocatalysts represent cost-effective and mild alternatives to photoredox catalysis; however, tuning their redox properties often requires complicated synthetic approach. Here we introduce N-heterocyclic carbene-triarylamine hybrids as novel donor-acceptor-type organophotocatalysts. These hybrids feature with facile structural modification, broad intramolecular charge-transfer absorption bands, and tunable redox potentials. Furthermore, these new photocatalysts have been successfully utilized for five distinct visible-light-induced redox-neutral radical cross-coupling reactions (94 examples, up to 99% yield). Mechanistic studies indicate that visible-light irradiation of the photocatalyst generates a charge-shifted excited state through photoinduced intramolecular electron transfer. This finding has a guiding significance for the design and development of new organophotocatalysts.
pool.authors: Wei Ding, Fang‐Yu Bian, Decheng Fu, Yu‐Jia Liu, Xin Li, Ying‐Feng Han

pool.title: Triple Combination Therapy: A Promising Path Forward against β-Lactamase-Mediated Resistance
pool.abstract: Abstract The silent pandemic of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to drive global morbidity and mortality. Resistance is often mediated by co-expression of serine β-lactamases (SBLs) and metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs), limiting treatment options. While several SBL inhibitors are clinically available, MBL inhibitors are yet to reach the market, and only a few candidates are in late-stage development. Dual-β-lactamase inhibitors remain an unmet goal. To preserve existing antibiotics, alternative strategies are required. This perspective highlights triple combination therapy comprising a β-lactam antibiotic, an SBL inhibitor, and an MBL-targeting agent to achieve broader coverage. Notably, in 2025, the U.S Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved aztreonam−avibactam (Emblaveo), in combination with metronidazole, for adults with complicated intra-abdominal infections who have limited or no alternative treatment options. Expanding such strategies may help mitigate AMR and support ongoing antimicrobial development efforts.
pool.authors: Nakita Reddy, José Rogério A. Silva, Per I. Arvidsson, Hendrik Gerhardus Kruger, Thavendran Govender, Tricia Naicker

pool.title: Recent advances in asymmetric electrochemical organocatalysis.
pool.abstract: The strategic integration of asymmetric organocatalysis with electroorganic synthesis has recently emerged as a versatile synthetic platform for the construction of chiral molecular scaffolds in a sustainable fashion. This review summarizes the research progress of asymmetric electrochemical organocatalysis from 2020 to 2026, covering its fundamental principles, mechanistic frameworks, and state-of-the-art advancements. Two core organocatalytic activation modes are systematically elaborated herein: covalent catalysis, represented by enamine catalysis and N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) catalysis, which generate catalytically active intermediates through covalent bonding; and non-covalent catalysis, which operates hydrogen bonding and ion pairing to activate substrates via weak interactions. The current challenges restricting the development of this field, including reaction compatibility, stereocontrol under electrochemical conditions, and synthetic scalability, are also discussed.
pool.authors: Hu H, Song L, Fu N

pool.title: Visible Light‐Driven NHC/Organophotoredox Catalysis: Mechanistic Insights and Organic Transformations
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT Visible light‐driven organophotoredox catalysis has emerged as a sustainable strategy for promoting diverse organic transformations with remarkable efficiency under mild reaction conditions. The integration of N‐heterocyclic carbene (NHC) catalysis with organophotoredox catalysis has enabled the generation of persistent ketyl radicals and transient radical intermediates through single electron transfer (SET), hydrogen atom transfer (HAT), and proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET) processes, thereby facilitating chemo‐, regio‐, and stereoselective Carbon–Carbon and C–heteroatom (N, O, P) bond‐forming reactions. Likewise, to overcome the limitations associated with transition‐metal‐based photocatalysts, sustainable metal‐free organophotoredox catalysts, such as xanthene dyes, acridinium salts, anthracene‐derived photocatalysts, and thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) donor–acceptor systems, have been extensively developed. Owing to their tunable photophysical properties, excellent redox capabilities, low toxicity, and cost‐effectiveness, these organophotoredox catalysts have emerged as attractive alternatives for transition metal‐based photoredox catalysis. This review summarizes the fundamental principles of visible light‐driven NHC/organophotoredox catalysis, discusses the underlying mechanistic pathways and dual catalytic transformations, thereby highlighting recent advances, their applications in late‐stage functionalization, current challenges, and future prospects in this rapidly evolving field.
pool.authors: Karthiyayini Gnanaoli, Merlin Abigail, Prema Sakthivel, C. Uma Maheswari

pool.title: Metal‐Free Synthesis of Oxa Spiro‐indene‐1,3‐dione Tetrahydrofurans and Pyrans via [3+2]/[4+2] Spirocyclization of 2‐Arylidene‐1,3‐indanedione With Haloalcohols
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT A concise and efficient method has been developed for the synthesis of pharmacologically important spiro‐indene‐1,3‐dione‐ fused tetrahydrofurans and pyrans via a base‐mediated cascade [3+2]/[4+2] spirocyclization of 2‐arylidene‐1,3‐indandiones and 2‐(3‐phenylallylidene)‐indandione with haloalcohols. This protocol offers several advantages, including a straightforward reaction process, short reaction times, broad substrate scope, high product yields, and mild, transition‐metal‐free reaction conditions. The practicality of this approach has been validated through gram‐scale synthesis, which furnished the desired products in good yields.
pool.authors: Soni Jagdeve, Suresh B. Waghmode

pool.title: Aromatic Pummerer‐Promoted Stereospecific Cross‐Coupling of Thiazoles With Boronic Esters
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT Thiazoles are ubiquitous motifs in bioactive molecules, making strategies for the stereospecific installation of chiral C(sp 3 )‐rich substituents on this scaffold particularly valuable for drug discovery. However, achieving such transformations remains nontrivial, as conventional C(sp 2 )–C(sp 3 ) cross‐coupling approaches are often compromised by catalyst deactivation and deleterious side reactions, such as β ‐hydride elimination. Although electrophile‐mediated coupling of alkyl boronic esters with lithiated aromatic compounds offers a potential route to C(sp 2 )–C(sp 3 ) bond formation, it is ineffective for thiazoles because the heteroaromatic core lacks sufficient nucleophilicity to engage electrophiles and promote productive 1,2‐migration. Herein, we report a lithiation–borylation–aromatic Pummerer (LiBAP) strategy that enables stereospecific C5 cross‐coupling of thiazoles with boronic esters. A pendant sulfinyl group enables exocyclic electrophilic activation, triggering a Pummerer‐type 1,2‐migration while avoiding unproductive C─B bond fragmentation. The reaction proceeds with complete stereospecificity and broad functional‐group tolerance, furnishing a C2 sulfide handle on thiazole that serves as a versatile linchpin for downstream C–S diversification. A formal asymmetric synthesis of a bioactive thiazole γ ‐secretase inhibitor was demonstrated to further highlight the synthetic utility of our LiBAP protocol.
pool.authors: Mark John P. Mandigma, Julien Lefranc, Louise Eagling, Jasper L. Tyler, Varinder Kumar Aggarwal

pool.title: Phenoxazinone synthase functional mimic activity of mixed-ligand copper(II) complexes of L-proline and diimine ligands conjugated with chitosan
pool.abstract: Abstract Phenoxazinone synthase (PHS) is a copper-containing bacterial enzyme that is involved in vital biological oxidation processes. Mimicking these enzymatic functions using copper complexes provides valuable insights and potential applications in green catalysis. In this work, chitosan-conjugated ligands were synthesized and anchored with Cu(II) to yield mixed-ligand complexes of the general formula [Cu(L)(bpy)(H2O)]2+ (1) and [Cu(L)(phen)(H2O)]2+ (2), where L represents chitosan-conjugated-proline polymer, and diimine ligands bpy and phen represent 2,2’-bipyridine and 1,10-phenanthroline, respectively. Fourier-transform infrared, scanning electron microscopy, powder X-ray diffraction, diffuse reflectance UV-visible (UV-vis) spectroscopy, thermogravimetric and differential thermal analyses and various spectroscopic methods were used to characterize the ligands and complexes. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry data revealed that complexes 1 and 2 contain 10.72% and 9.81% of copper, respectively. The oxidation of o-aminophenol (OAP), a model substrate, monitored by UV-vis spectrophotometry, provides valuable kinetic and mechanistic insights into substrate interactions. Interestingly, among the complexes, 2 exhibited the highest catalytic activity, featuring phenanthroline as a co-ligand, followed by 1 and then ligand (L), highlighting the influence of the co-ligands on the oxidation of o-aminophenol to phenoxazinone, a functional mimic of phenoxazinone enzyme. Notably, complex 2 demonstrates 72% conversion of OAP to 2-aminophenoxazine-3-one. Kinetic analysis revealed pseudo-first-order rate constants consistent with efficient oxidase mimics. These results demonstrate the potential of Cu-chitosan hybrids as sustainable, bioinspired catalysts.
pool.authors: Liji Muthirakalayil Abraham, Manikandan Varadhan, Kugan Mahalingam, Thangaraja Chinnathangavel, Venugopal Rajendiran

pool.title: Difluoromethylenation of Alkynes: Streamlined Access to Allyl Difluorides
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT A direct difluoromethylenation of alkynes has been developed using HF/pyridine as a dual acidic and fluorinating medium. The reaction proceeds via in situ generation of a primary oxocarbenium ion from formaldehyde, enabling efficient formation of two C(sp 3 )─F bonds and one C(sp 2 )═C(sp 2 ) bond in a single step without the need for pre‐functionalized reagents. This strategy offers a concise route to allyl difluorides as a complementary approach to incorporate difluoromethylene motifs into complex molecular frameworks. Additional spectroscopic and computational investigations provide insights into this mechanism.
pool.authors: Fabien Naullet, Sourav Mondal, Frédéric Guégan, Bastien Michelet, Sébastien Thibaudeau

pool.title: Structural Diversification of Fangchinoline via a CuAAC Reaction: Design, Batch and Semi‐Flow Synthesis, and Anticancer Activity Evaluation
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT In this study, we reported late‐stage structural diversification of fangchinoline (FC) via a CuAAC method to incorporate multifunctional 1,2,3‐triazole scaffolds. A series of new C7‐substituted FC derivatives were designed, synthesized, and evaluated as anticancer agents. Considering the superior heat and mass transfer characteristics of flow chemistry, we also employed a practical modification strategy of FC with higher yields in a simple loop reactor. Notably, FC01 , FC03 , and FC05 exhibited high antitumor activities against HeLa, MCF‐7, and HCT‐116 cells, respectively. These three compounds demonstrated two to fourfold greater potency than the parent compounds tetrandrine and FC. Although 1,2,3‐triazole and carbamate were both recognized as amide bioisosteres, in contrast to FC derivatives bearing carbamate linkage on C7 position, the better anticancer activities of 1,2,3‐triazole‐containing compounds indicated that both the linkage and side chain provided major contributions to cytotoxicity activities. These results were further confirmed by molecular docking with protein kinase C‐α. In addition, pharmacological assays revealed that FC05 could inhibit proliferation and induce apoptosis, as well as arrest the cell cycle of HCT‐116 cell lines at G0/G1 phase arrest with concentration‐dependent effects.
pool.authors: Shuai Zhang, Chang Liu, Jiahao Zhang, Chengyu Sun, Yang Yu, Hao Li

pool.title: Electricity-Driven Radical Carbonyl Catalysis for Asymmetric Synthesis of α-Tertiary Amino Esters.
pool.abstract: Electrochemistry has become a powerful and environmentally sustainable tool for driving redox transformations in modern chemical synthesis. However, achieving stereocontrol in electrocatalysis remains a persistent challenge. Introducing asymmetric organocatalysis into electrosynthesis offers an attractive strategy for controlling enantioselectivity, though successful systems to date are very limited. This limitation largely stems from several key factors, including the highly polar electrochemical environment, which can weaken noncovalent interactions, and the transient, highly reactive nature of radical intermediates, both of which complicate enantiocontrol. Employing chiral pyridoxal as a catalyst, we have successfully developed a novel asymmetric electrocatalytic system. This system facilitates an electricity-driven, asymmetric oxidative coupling of amino acid esters with silyl enol ethers through radical carbonyl catalysis. The method enables the efficient synthesis of biologically significant α-tertiary amino acid esters with good yields and excellent stereoselectivities. Beyond efficiently activating the amino acid esters, the chiral pyridoxal catalyst also delivers exceptional enantiocontrol even under highly polar reaction conditions, establishing an efficient organocatalytic platform for asymmetric electrosynthesis.
pool.authors: Tao Y, Li J, Yu R, Zheng J, Chen T, Liu S, Zhang L, Zhao B

pool.title: Activation of Allylic Primary Alcohols With Biaryl Oxazepine Reagent for Chiral Phosphoric Acid-Catalyzed Asymmetric SN1 Reaction.
pool.abstract: Carbocations have long been important reactive intermediates in organic synthesis. Nevertheless, their inherent instability and high reactivity present formidable challenges to achieving precise stereocontrol. Previous strategies require the chiral catalyst to establish an optimal chiral environment around the carbocations, thus, high enantioselectivity can be obtained in these SN1 reactions. Herein, we report a chiral phosphoric acid (CPA)-catalyzed SN1 reaction of primary allylic alcohol, in which the leaving group can modulate the reactivity and control enantioselectivity by forming a complex with the chiral catalyst. The key to the success of this reaction is the development of an alcohol activation reagent (biaryl oxazepine), which can chemoselectively activate allylic alcohol to form an intermediate with good leaving ability. A series of allylic 5,6-dihydrophenanthridine and 6H-benzo[c]chromene products could be obtained in high yields with excellent enantioselectivities. Further transformations and applications of the resulting 5,6-dihydrophenanthridine derivatives and the asymmetric formal total synthesis of several natural products demonstrated the utilities of this reaction. Mechanistic studies support that the reaction proceeds via an SN1 pathway, in which the enantio-control of allyl carbocations was achieved by in situ formed complex from chiral catalysts and leaving groups.
pool.authors: Yuan W, Duan A, Zhu B, Dai G, Huang T, Tan W, Xu L, Shen B, Yang X

pool.title: Organocatalytic Formal (3+2+1)-Cycloaddition of Allenoates, Michael Acceptors, and Carbaldehydes.
pool.abstract: Employing secondary amines as covalently interacting Lewis basic organocatalysts allows for the activation of electron-deficient allenes (allenoates) for unprecedented formal (3+2+1)-cycloadditions with Michael acceptors and aromatic carbaldehydes. This strategy is proposed to proceed via nucleophilic addition of the catalyst to the allenoate's β-carbon first, followed by γ-addition to the Michael acceptor, a subsequent aldol-type step, and the final ring closure and catalyst liberation. Hereby, direct access to various highly functionalized spirocyclic cyclohexanone-derivatives (17 examples) in good to excellent yields (up to 98%) and a first proof-of-concept for an asymmetric variant (around 75:25 er) by using chiral secondary amine catalysts has been obtained as well.
pool.authors: Naderer D, Pötscher A, Eder K, Monkowius U, Himmelsbach M, Waser M

pool.title: A recyclable copper catalyst with mPEG-supported chiral Schiff base ligands for the asymmetric Henry reaction and drug synthesis.
pool.abstract: The asymmetric Henry reaction represents a powerful method for constructing chiral β-nitro alcohols; however, most existing catalytic systems suffer from poor recyclability, which limits their sustainable application. To address this challenge, based on the concept of green organocatalysis, this study is dedicated to developing a novel recyclable chiral catalytic system. A dual-core design strategy was adopted: (i) methoxy polyethylene glycol, which exhibits good biocompatibility, was selected as an environmentally friendly carrier; (ii) readily available L-tert-leucine was used as the precursor of the chiral catalytic center. A novel methoxy polyethylene glycol-supported chiral Schiff base ligand, L12, was successfully prepared. This ligand, in cooperation with copper acetate, facilitated the construction of a rationally designed catalytic system that exhibits remarkable activity for asymmetric Henry reactions. The system enables the efficient synthesis of various chiral β-nitro alcohols with considerable stereoselectivity. Notably, the catalytic system demonstrates satisfactory recyclability, further enhancing its practical value. Based on these performance advantages, the system shows significant application potential in the synthesis of chiral drug molecules and active intermediates. Overall, this work not only provides an efficient and recyclable protocol for the green synthesis of chiral β-nitro alcohols, but also offers a promising route for the sustainable preparation of key intermediates in chiral drug synthesis, highlighting its potential for industrial application.
pool.authors: Liu Q, Han G, Zhao J, Zhang S, Wang S, He W

pool.title: Catalytic asymmetric reactions of isoxazole derivatives: organocatalysis, metal catalysis and phase-transfer catalysis.
pool.abstract: Isoxazoles are versatile N,O-containing five-membered heterocyclic building blocks widely utilized in the construction of chiral pharmaceutical intermediates. Over the past two decades, tremendous progress has been made in their catalytic asymmetric transformations, which can be categorized into three types: organocatalysis, transition-metal catalysis and chiral phase-transfer catalysis, yet a systematic review covering all these systems remains absent. This paper summarizes diverse reactions involving substrates such as nitroalkenylisoxazoles and aminoisoxazoles, including asymmetric Michael addition, cycloaddition, cascade addition, ring contraction and hydrofunctionalization. It elaborates on reaction parameters, substrate compatibility, stereocontrol mechanisms and synthetic practicability of each catalytic system and compares the respective merits and drawbacks of the three catalytic categories. This review identifies the existing limitations in this research field and puts forward prospects for future development, providing a theoretical reference for the exploration of novel asymmetric catalytic reactions based on isoxazole scaffolds.
pool.authors: Li L, Loh TP

profiles.intent: Microbial communities, interactions and biogeochemical functions in oceans, seawater and marine sediments.

pool.title: Making waves: Rethinking antiscalants in seawater desalination - Balancing scaling control, biofouling risk, and ecological consequences.
pool.abstract: Antiscalants used in reverse osmosis (RO) desalination are commonly treated as simple operational additives, yet their chemical properties can significantly influence microbial dynamics, thereby creating a critical operational paradox. While antiscalants inhibit mineral scaling, they may simultaneously promote biofouling through poorly resolved mechanisms. Current vendor-driven selection prioritizes scaling control but overlooks microbial and environmental consequences. This opacity obscures molecular composition, impurity profiles, and transformation pathways, introducing uncertainty across the desalination lifecycle. Undisclosed chemical composition limits risk assessment, while interactions with marine microbial communities that drive biofouling lack mechanistic clarity. Emerging evidence indicates that antiscalants can both stimulate microbial growth via orthophosphate impurities, a readily bioavailable inorganic phosphorus source, and labile organic fractions, but may also inhibit growth through trace metal sequestration, particularly the sequestration of bioavailable iron, a metabolically essential micronutrient. The contribution of this inhibitory mechanism under seawater desalination conditions remains to be quantified. The net outcome is formulation-specific and environmental context-dependent. Beyond the treatment plant, the fate and impacts of discharged antiscalants remain insufficiently constrained, introducing uncertainty for marine ecosystems. We argue that antiscalant selection should shift from empirical practices to a predictive, mechanism-based strategy. Accordingly, we propose a Predictive Ecological Chemistry framework grounded in three principles: transparent chemical characterization, mechanistic evaluation of microbial responses, and environmental accountability. This framework offers a pathway toward data-driven selection that balances operational performance with ecological responsibility.
pool.authors: Gonzalez-Gil G, Castrillón-Tobón M, Ruiz MCA, Das R, Altmann T, Vrouwenvelder JS

pool.title: Integrated assessment of bioplastic materials effects on microbial communities and macroinvertebrate model, Mytilus galloprovincialis, in marine ecosystems.
pool.abstract: The increasing use of biopolymer derivatives raises concerns about their actual environmental sustainability, which remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we adopted an integrated approach combining microbial and ecotoxicological perspectives to evaluate their impact in marine ecosystems. We investigated the plastisphere composition of conventional petroleum-based High Density Polyethylene (HDPE) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), polyhydroxybutyric acid (PHB), and polylactic acid (PLLA) scaffolds after 60 days of exposition in marine ecosystem or microcosm, by high throughput metagenomics 16S rRNA gene sequencing and culture dependent approach. A variation in terms of composition and abundance of plastisphere, between petroleum-derived and bio-based degradable scaffolds, was observed. A high abundance of Proteobacteria was detected in all polymers, with Alpha and Gamma Proteobacteria dominant. At the genera level, high abundance of sequences assigned to hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria (i.e. Oleibacter, Labrenzia, Alcanivorax) was detected in biopolymeric plastic compared to petroleum-based plastic. To link microbial colonization and material degradation with biological effects on marine fauna, the impact of biopolymer-derived micro- and nanoparticles on the mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis was assessed. Both in vitro and in vivo assays demonstrated immune system activation through phagocytosis and encapsulation, while in vivo exposures influenced several biomarkers (phagocytosis, haemocyte density, lysozyme, glutathione peroxidase, phenoloxidase, alkaline phosphatase, esterase), suggesting potential detrimental effects after 72 h. By bridging microbial ecology with immunological responses in a bioindicator species, this multidisciplinary study provides novel insights into the complex ecological footprint of biodegradable plastics in marine environments.
pool.authors: Dara M, Calabrisotto LS, Bisanti L, Torreagrossa N, La Corte C, Bertini F, Catania V, Quatrini P, Parrinello D, Piazzese D, Cammarata M, Banni M, Parisi MG

pool.title: Temperate marine macrophytes are highly variable sources of Biogenic Volatile Organic Compounds – a comparative study from the Baltic Sea and NE Atlantic
pool.abstract: Abstract. Biogenic Volatile Organic Compounds (BVOC), emitted by Earth’s ecosystems, affect several chemical processes in the atmosphere that have profound climate impacts. Despite their climate relevance, global BVOC budget estimations are still highly uncertain, with ocean-derived emissions being particularly poorly constrained. Marine macrophytes (i.e. macroalgae and seagrass) are a large and widespread organismal group whose BVOC emission rates are particularly poorly quantified. In this study, we set out to address this knowledge gap by quantifying ex situ the BVOC emission rates of three temperate macrophytes (Zostera marina, Fucus vesiculosus and Ulva intestinalis) with a Vocus proton-transfer-reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometer (Vocus PTR-TOF). To capture and improve our understanding of the variability of macrophyte BVOC emissions, our quantifications were repeated across two contrasting coastal regions: the northeastern Atlantic (Ireland) and northern Baltic Sea (Finland). The three macrophytes emitted a wide range of BVOCs, with a total of 166 different compounds detected. Although many BVOCs were emitted by all macrophytes, significant differences were observed in the total emission profiles, both between and within species. Interestingly, the seagrass Zostera exhibited significantly higher overall BVOC emission rates per unit biomass than the two macroalgae and showed clearly differing intraspecific emission profiles across the two regions. Regarding individual compounds, dimethyl sulfide (DMS) was emitted at the highest rates, but many other compounds (e.g., sesquiterpenes and C10H21O+) also displayed notable emission rates. Although many of the observed BVOCs are commonly investigated compounds (e.g., DMS and terpenoids), our results show that macrophyte BVOC emissions comprise a large number of different compounds, suggesting that future studies would benefit from targeting a wider range of BVOCs than currently considered. Our results highlight macrophytes as highly variable sources of BVOCs, whose better inclusion into marine BVOC budgets should be strived for. However, more robust data are needed, and future research should also focus on investigating the dynamics driving macrophyte BVOC emissions, their variability, and their eventual fate in the environment.
pool.authors: Max L. E. Gräfnings, Yuanyuan Luo, Jian Zhao, Claudia L. Cara-Ortega, Kirsten N. Fossum, Frans Graeffe, Lu Lei, Dagmar Brigitte Stengel, Roseline C. Thakur, Jurgita Ovadnevaitė, Mikael Ehn, Camilla Gustafsson

pool.title: Life at the edge: Planktic foraminiferal distribution through the California Current Oxygen Minimum Zone
pool.abstract: Abstract Oxygen Minimum Zones (OMZs) are expanding globally, reshaping marine ecosystems, and creating physiologically challenging conditions for many marine organisms. Vulnerable communities will likely shift toward taxa adapted to low-oxygen conditions. Such adaptations are rare in eukaryotes, but some foraminiferal taxa can survive, and even calcify, in severely oxygen-depleted environments. Foraminiferal tests in marine sediments provide an archive of OMZ variability across past climate transitions; however, the modern oxygen and depth habitat of planktic foraminifera remain underexplored, particularly compared to their benthic counterparts. Here, we present the first depth-stratified, seasonal, and multi-station observations of planktic foraminifera within an OMZ paired with in situ oxygen measurements. Plankton tows (0-900 m) across five stations in the California Current System (CCS) during autumn 2023 and spring 2024 revealed distinct vertical niches for OMZ-associated species. Known OMZ-dweller, Globorotaloides hexagonus , occurred at all stations and showed comparable depth-integrated densities during autumn and spring with an average living depth (ALD) of 367-587 m. Generalized additive models (GAMs) indicated that oxygen’s partial effect on live (cytoplasm-bearing) G. hexagonus density peaked within hypoxic waters (55 µmol kg -1 ) with populations persisting at 16 µmol kg -1 . These results confirm that G. hexagonus is primarily restricted to hypoxic waters, expanding this understanding across latitudinal, seasonal, and spatial gradients in the CCS. Occupying a vertical niche above G. hexagonus , the planktic foraminifer Globorotalia scitula consistently occurred at highest density within the upper oxycline, surviving in waters as low as 27 µmol kg -1 . As the first study to constrain the in situ oxygen habitat of G. scitula , these findings establish its potential as a proxy for upper-oxycline dynamics. These characterizations of depth habitat and associated oxygen conditions for deep-dwelling planktic foraminifera in OMZs will improve reconstructions of mid-depth oxygenation in the geologic record and further understanding of potential ‘winners’ in an increasingly deoxygenated ocean.
pool.authors: Rachel Alcorn, Karen F. Wishner, Lily Ramos, Bernhard Joan M., Fatma Gomaa, Scott D. Wankel, Catherine V. Davis

pool.title: Salt marsh porewater alkalinity varies with plant species identity and growth stage
pool.abstract: Salt marshes are increasingly recognized as important sources of total alkalinity (TA), contributing to coastal carbon sequestration. While hydrological drivers are well studied, plant-mediated effects on TA export remain poorly constrained. Here, we assess how plant species identity and diversity influence TA production in a marsh mesocosm experiment including eight species and two- and five-species mixtures. On average, porewater TA concentrations were nearly twice as high in vegetated sediments (~4200 µmol kg - ¹) compared to unvegetated controls (~2400 µmol kg - ¹). However, responses varied strongly among species, with monocultures ranging from values comparable to unvegetated sediments (e.g., Puccinellia maritima ) to >5000 µmol kg - ¹ ( Triglochin maritima ). TA increased with plant growth stage, belowground biomass, sediment water content, and more reducing soil conditions, indicating tight coupling between plant traits and sediment biogeochemistry. However, TA did not increase consistently with plant species richness, as mixtures generally converged toward intermediate values. Lower TA production was often associated with higher TA:DIC ratios, suggesting a greater relative buffering capacity despite lower absolute alkalinity generation. These findings suggest that species identity and development may be important factors influencing salt marsh alkalinity production, with implications for coastal carbonate dynamics and blue carbon budgets.
pool.authors: Nienke Mueller, Ella Lu Logemann, Gloria M. S. Reithmaier

pool.title: Weathering-derived calcium supports carbon storage in grassland soils
pool.abstract: Abstract Dark colored grassland soils, known as Mollisols, are intensively farmed and rich in organic matter, and hence have an important role in the carbon cycle. Organic carbon storage in Mollisols may result from interactions between organic matter and calcium released by carbonate and silicate weathering. Here we test this hypothesis by using a geochemical model to simulate calcium release from weathering in soils across the USA. We find that calcium released by mineral weathering is associated with soil organic carbon storage and that this effect is stronger in Mollisols than in non-Mollisols. Our model also shows that agriculture has increased calcium inputs to cultivated USA Mollisols 4-5 fold, indicating that humans have fundamentally changed the geochemical conditions that sustain organic carbon in these soils. By implication, moderating the quantity of and timing of calcium release may help to preserve and restore carbon in the world’s most intensively farmed landscapes.
pool.authors: E. W. Slessarev, H. R. Goertzen, Rebecca A. Lybrand, Karis J. McFarlane, Jennifer Pett‐Ridge, Noah W. Sokol, D. G. Zaharescu, K. Georgiou

pool.title: MANGOSTEEN (GARCINIA MANGOSTANA L.) PERICARP EXTRACT REDUCES SYSTEMIC MICROPLASTIC BURDEN BY PRESERVING INTESTINAL DEFENSE MECHANISMS IN POLYETHYLENE MICROPLASTIC-EXPOSED RATS
pool.abstract: Growing evidence indicates that ingested microplastics can disrupt intestinal barrier integrity and promote their translocation into systemic circulation, potentially leading to adverse health effects.This study investigated the protective effects of mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana L.) peel extract against the intestinal translocation of polyethylene microplastics in a Wistar rat model.A controlled in vivo experiment was conducted using thirty-five male Wistar rats randomly allocated into five groups: a negative control group, a polyethylene microplastic-exposed group (5 mg/day), and three treatment groups receiving Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana L.) Pericarp Extract Reduces Systemic Microplastic Burden by Preserving Intestinal Defense Mechanisms in Polyethylene Microplastic-Exposed Rats IJDDT Volume 16 Issue 65s 2026 Page: 1866 polyethylene microplastics combined with mangosteen peel extract at doses of 200, 400, and 600 mg/kg body weight/day for 28 consecutive days.Polyethylene microplastic exposure significantly increased circulating microplastic particle counts in the blood and was associated with compromised intestinal barrier function.Treatment with mangosteen peel extract resulted in a dose-dependent reduction in blood microplastic levels.The protective effects were accompanied by increased total culturable gut microbiome abundance, enhanced fecal immunoglobulin A secretion, improved goblet cell density and mucus production, and elevated epithelial superoxide dismutase expression (all, p<0.05).These findings provide mechanistic evidence supporting the potential use of mangosteen-derived bioactive compounds as natural protective agents against microplastic-induced intestinal dysfunction and systemic exposure.

pool.title: Reptiles in the One Health ecology of antimicrobial resistance, with insights into zoonotic pathogens: reservoirs, transmission pathways, and public health implications
pool.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a growing global health challenge at the interface of human, animal, and environmental health. Reptiles—including wild populations, pets, farmed species, and internationally traded animals—are increasingly recognized as participants in One Health AMR networks, occupying ecological interfaces that facilitate interactions among wildlife, domestic animals, humans, and the environment. Their diverse microbiota and exposure to both natural and anthropogenically influenced habitats create opportunities for the acquisition and dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (AMR bacteria) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), particularly in captive settings where close human contact and husbandry practices may favor bacterial exchange. Recent studies demonstrate that reptiles frequently harbor clinically relevant ARGs encoding extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBL), AmpC-β-lactamases, carbapenemases, and colistin resistance. Potential exposure pathways include direct contact, bites, environmental contamination of terraria and husbandry systems, and, in some regions, the handling and consumption of reptile-derived food products. Wild reptiles may additionally serve as valuable sentinels for anthropogenic AMR pollution within terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Despite growing interest, the role of reptiles within the broader ecology of AMR remains incompletely understood. Available studies are geographically uneven, methodologically heterogeneous, and frequently lack high-resolution genomic characterization, limiting robust assessment of transmission pathways, transmission directionality, and the relative contribution of reptiles compared with other wildlife and environmental reservoirs. This review synthesizes current evidence on the occurrence, diversity, and transmission of AMR bacteria in reptiles and discusses their implications for public health, veterinary medicine, wildlife conservation, and One Health. It further highlights major methodological limitations, critical knowledge gaps, and priorities for harmonized, genomics-informed surveillance. Overall, current evidence suggests that reptiles should be viewed as ecologically relevant participants in the One Health ecology of antimicrobial resistance, although their relative contribution to AMR dissemination remains to be quantified.
pool.authors: Christa Ewers, Franziska Unger, Ellen Prenger‐Berninghoff, Tobias Eisenberg

pool.title: Hierarchical physiological sensitivity of the coral, Orbicella faveolata, to suspended sediment and elevated temperature
pool.abstract: Abstract Coral reefs are increasingly exposed to multiple environmental stressors, including ocean warming and elevated turbidity from coastal development, dredging, and sediment resuspension. Understanding how these stressors affect coral physiology is essential for improving sediment management and protecting reef ecosystems. We investigated the short-term physiological responses of the Caribbean reef-building coral, Orbicella faveolata , to suspended sediment and elevated temperature during controlled 72-h laboratory experiments. Coral fragments were first exposed in independent chamber–sump systems to a gradient of target turbidity levels consisting of a control with no added sediment and treatments of 15, 29, and 50 NTU, followed by a factorial experiment evaluating suspended sediment (control or 29 NTU) and temperature (27°C or 30°C). Metabolic oxygen flux was quantified using intermittent-flow respirometry; photophysiological performance was assessed using pulse-amplitude-modulated fluorometry, and tissue and skeletal condition were evaluated using biological and calcification endpoints. Elevated temperature produced the most consistent responses, decreasing maximum photochemical efficiency (Fv/Fm), increasing regulated non-photochemical energy dissipation (YNPQ), and altering respiration. Suspended sediment elicited comparatively limited responses, primarily affecting photophysiological metrics, with modest effects on respiration in the highest-turbidity treatment. No suspended sediment × temperature interaction was detected. Net calcification, symbiont density, chlorophyll concentration, and host protein content remained largely unchanged across treatments, while genotype accounted for significant variation in multiple physiological responses. Collectively, these findings support a hierarchy of short-term physiological sensitivity, with photophysiological metrics showing the most consistent responses, metabolic responses being more limited, and biomass-related and skeletal-growth endpoints remaining largely stable over the 72-h exposure. Integrating photophysiological measurements into monitoring programs may improve early detection of sublethal coral stress during coastal and climate-related disturbances.
pool.authors: Keisha D. Bahr, Robert J. Bretzing-Tungate, Briana M. Matthews, Eleanor G. TenBrink, Casey L. Gallagher, Abigail Libbin Cannon

pool.title: Cobamide-based interactions between soil bacteria can be predicted based on monoculture growth
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT Interactions between microbes shape the structure and function of microbial communities. While studying interactions is key to understanding microbial communities as a whole, gaining a detailed mechanistic view is challenging due to the number of co-occurring interactions. Here, we focus on a single class of shared nutrients, the cobalamin (vitamin B 12 ) family of enzyme cofactors known as cobamides, to study nutrient interactions in laboratory consortia of increasing complexity. Measuring cobamide-dependent growth of two soil Caulobacter isolates in monoculture revealed that each grows faster within a distinct range of cobamide concentrations. Co-culturing the two isolates demonstrated that the cobamide concentration predictably determines which isolate predominates. These results suggest that, although the two organisms appear functionally redundant, with identical metabolic capabilities predicted in their genomes, they may occupy distinct niches in their environment based on cobamide concentration. We further examined the ability of cobamide-producing Mesorhizobium and Priestia isolates to share cobamides and found that both support the cobamide-dependent growth of the two Caulobacter isolates. The Caulobacter isolates could coexist in tri-cultures with each producer following serial passaging, indicating the producers can support the growth of multiple cobamide-dependent organisms. We analyzed the metabolic capacity encoded in the genomes of the four isolates and found that cobamides are likely the main shared nutrient in our co- and tri-cultures. These results highlight the utility of cobamides as a model nutrient to characterize and predict interactions in bacterial consortia of increasing complexity. IMPORTANCE Interactions between microbes shape their communities and the world around them. Because microbial communities are physically and chemically complex, predicting microbial interactions is often difficult. Using a set of four bacteria isolated from the same soil environment, we generated and tested predictions about the interactions involving a family of model nutrients related to cobalamin (vitamin B 12 ). Understanding and predicting interactions can lead to greater insights into microbiome function.
pool.authors: Zoila I. Alvarez-Aponte, Hazel I. Anagu, Kenny C. Mok, Sandy T. Nguyen, Valentine V. Trotter, Michiko E. Taga

pool.title: Synoptic and regional-scale meteorological controls of stratus altitude in the Namib Desert
pool.abstract: Abstract. In the Namib Desert, fog is an essential water source and occurs when and where advected marine stratus clouds intersect with the land surface. However, the meteorological controls of the cloud base height are still insufficiently understood. This study aims to develop a basic understanding of the relevant processes. We combine satellite and in situ observations with large-scale meteorological data from reanalysis data (ERA5) to compare fog events to lifted stratus at the coast (low-cloud events). In fog situations, the marine boundary layer is shallower along the entire coastline than in low-cloud situations. This is found to be related to the large-scale high-pressure systems. Fog situations exhibit a weaker Atlantic High but elevated continental pressure. The weaker Atlantic High is connected to less pronounced near-surface winds along the coastline, less cold advection, and heat fluxes upstream of the study region, leading to the shallower marine boundary layer. Increased continental pressure facilitates the development of regional mountain-plain winds that may reduce the height of the coastal inversion. These mechanisms are highlighted in a case study of an off-season fog event. To assess the predictive power of the two high-pressure systems and the regional pressure pattern, a logistic regression is trained with three corresponding features. The classification outperformed a climatological baseline by ≈ 10 %, suggesting that the features contain relevant process information. The results improve our understanding of the processes that determine the seasonal and day-to-day variability of fog versus elevated low-cloud occurrence in the Namib.
pool.authors: Viola Hipler, Hendrik Andersen, Robert Spirig, R. Vogt, Stuart Piketh, Bianca Adler, Jan Čermák

pool.title: Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
pool.abstract: Abstract. The importance of carbon storage in continental seafloor sediments is increasingly recognized, yet the role of benthic macrofaunal biodiversity in the regulation of these processes remains poorly understood. Benthic macrofauna contributes to organic carbon cycling through respiration and secondary production, while the sediment reworking (bioturbation) and ventilation (bioirrigation) of infauna promote the redistribution and remineralization of organic matter in sediments. Here, we investigated how benthic community structure, functional traits, and the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling vary along environmental gradients in muddy sediments of the southeastern North Sea. Based on 171 macrofaunal taxa collected from 50 stations, a cluster analysis revealed a clear spatial structuring of the benthic macrofauna communities across the study region. The community composition was primarily structured by bottom shear stress, salinity, and sediment characteristics. Further, a functional trait analysis showed a clear shift in community composition with water depth. Communities in the deeper sections of the study area were dominated by mobile biodiffusors and subsurface filter feeders, whereas shallower communities were characterized by less mobile, surface-modifying bivalves and polychaetes. These contrasting patterns led to pronounced differences in ecosystem functioning: bioturbation and bioirrigation potentials were significantly higher in deeper communities, whereas community secondary production and respiration were higher in shallow communities. Across all stations, community secondary production and respiration increased with taxonomic and functional diversity, while bioturbation and bioirrigation potentials were negatively related to diversity and community evenness, reflecting a dominance by key bioturbating taxa. Our findings demonstrate that environmental gradients fundamentally shape both benthic community structure and the nature of the link between biodiversity and essential ecosystem functions. These results contribute to our understanding of the role macrofauna can play in processes related to carbon sequestration in marine deposition centers with fine-grained sediment and organic matter in shelf sea systems.
pool.authors: Chueh-Chen Tung, Moritz Holtappels, Alexa Wrede, Male Köster, Lasse Sander, Jan Beermann, Vera Sidorenko, Lars Gutow

pool.title: Mycosphere microbiome assembly and metabolic reprogramming in Phallus rugulosus revealed by multi-omics integration
pool.abstract: The mycosphere, defined as the soil zone influenced by fungal hyphae, hosts a distinct microbiome that plays a critical role in host development. Nevertheless, the assembly rules and metabolic functions in macrofungi remain poorly understood. This study aims to disentangle these processes in the edible fungus Phallus rugulosus . We integrated metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and untargeted metabolomics to compare mycosphere soil (MS) and bulk soil (BS) of P. rugulosus . No significant differences in alpha-diversity were detected between MS and BS, whereas beta diversity analysis showed significant separation. The MS harbored significantly enriched saprotrophic fungi and bacteria whose functional gene profiles pointed to involvement in anaerobic carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling (e.g., Patescibacteria, Fibrobacterota, Thermodesulfobacteriota). Functional profiling indicated a metabolic shift from aerobic respiration to anaerobic fermentation and coupled nitrification–denitrification within the mycosphere. Metabolomics identified 254 up-regulated metabolites in the MS, including a signaling-molecule (indole-3-carboxaldehyde) and defense-related compounds (dihydrodaidzein). Network analysis identified Module 1, dominated by Patescibacteria and Fibrobacterota, as a core discriminative signature (AUC = 0.92). Partial least squares path-modeling (PLS-PM, GOF = 0.836) revealed strong positive associations among the mycosphere effect, soil fertility, microbial restructuring, functional gene expression, and metabolite accumulation, revealing a hierarchical cascade propagating from soil properties through microbial communities and functional genes to metabolite profiles. These findings are consistent with the three hypotheses that P. rugulosus enriches specific microbial taxa, that functional gene expression shows coordinated changes with these taxa, and that these components form an interconnected microbe–gene–metabolite network. This multi-omics framework advances our understanding of fungus-microbe interactions and provides reference information for future optimization of edible-mushroom cultivation systems.
pool.authors: Liu Miao, Yang Wang, Kai Huang, Qingzhong Meng, Xiaoxuan You, Rubing Tian, Xuanang Zhang, Bilinyi Zhao, Ling Li, Wenxin Jiang, Minglei Li

pool.title: Integrated in vitro and in silico evaluation of the antibiofilm activity of Artemisia dracunculus L. against Pseudomonas aeruginosa
pool.abstract: This study investigated the antibiofilm and antibacterial potential of Artemisia dracunculus L. extract through integrated in vitro and in silico approaches. Antibacterial activity was evaluated using the disc diffusion method against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus subtilis, and Bacillus licheniformis while antibiofilm activity was determined by crystal violet assay. The extract exhibited promising antibiofilm activity at the tested concentration against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In terms of antibacterial activity, the strongest effect was detected against the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis, with an inhibition zone diameter of 9.95±0.45 mm. To explore the possible molecular basis of these effects, chlorogenic acid and kaempferol were subjected to molecular docking analyses against LasR (transcriptional regulator) and anthranilate–coenzyme A ligase (PqsA). Chlorogenic acid and kaempferol showed favorable binding affinities, with docking scores ranging from -7.27 to –9.23 kcal/mol, indicating strong interactions with the active sites of both proteins. Overall, the results demonstrate that Artemisia dracunculus represents a promising natural source of bioactive compounds for controlling biofilm-associated infections. Further studies involving compound isolation, mechanistic confirmation, and in vivo validation are recommended.
pool.authors: Suzan Şahin Doğan

pool.title: Effects of natural environmental drivers and different mobile bottom-contact fishing intensity on infauna communities in NATURA 2000 sites in the German Exclusive Economic Zone of the North Sea
pool.abstract: Three marine protected areas, i.e., Borkum Reef Ground, Sylt Outer Reef, and Dogger Bank, have been established within the European NATURA 2000 program in the German Exclusive Economic Zone of the North Sea. Within them, we analysed the effect of the varying impact of mobile bottom-contact fishing on infauna communities in selected focus areas as a baseline study prior to the exclusion of mobile bottom-contact fishing since 2023. The three focus areas varied significantly in sediment composition and depth. The mobile bottom-contact fishing intensity was lowest at Borkum Reef Ground, but revealed decreasing gradients at Sylt Outer Reef and Dogger Bank. The infauna communities in the three focus areas were significantly different. Gradients in sediment composition, e.g. sand, mud, gravel and shell contents, revealed significant relationships with the infauna communities in the three areas. But on a small spatial scale also the gradients of mobile bottom-contact fishing intensity correlated significantly with the variations of the infauna communities at Sylt Outer Reef and Dogger Bank. The common agreement of the European Commission for the exclusion of mobile bottom-contact fishing in parts of Borkum Reef Ground and Sylt Outer Reef since 2023 and of Dogger Bank since 2025 will provide the opportunity to study the recovery of the infauna communities in these areas from mobile bottom-contact fishing in future.
pool.authors: Ramona Ohde, Ingrid Kröncke

pool.title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design
pool.abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.
pool.authors: Enes Üstüner, Mustafa Öz

pool.title: Mitigating zoonotic pathogens in the food supply chain: veterinary strategies and biosensor technologies for ensuring the safety of animal-derived products
pool.abstract: Zoonotic diseases, which are transmitted from animals to humans, represent a major global public health concern, particularly through the consumption of contaminated animal-derived food products such as meat, dairy, eggs, and seafood. These foods, while nutritionally essential, can act as carriers of pathogenic microorganisms, such as Brucella , Listeria , Campylobacter , and Salmonella . This review explores the risk of zoonotic pathogens in the food supply chain and presents an integrated approach to control contamination at various stages of food production and distribution. Key strategies include pre-harvest controls on farms, such as improved husbandry, vaccination, and biosecurity measures; post-harvest interventions aimed at reducing microbial contamination during slaughter, processing, storage, and transport; and the promotion of hygienic food handling and distribution practices. At the consumer level, education and awareness campaigns play a critical role in reducing foodborne infections. Furthermore, continuous monitoring through veterinary inspections and pathogen surveillance enables early detection of and response to outbreaks. The adoption of food safety standards, regulatory frameworks, and advanced traceability systems, enhanced by biosensor technologies, further strengthens food safety management. These coordinated efforts are essential for ensuring the safety of animal-derived foods, preventing zoonotic disease transmission, and safeguarding public health.
pool.authors: Xiaohui Liang, Chang Xu, Tingting Sun, Sijia Lu, Kun Li, Lizeng Peng

pool.title: Biofilm‐Mediated Persistence of Salmonella in Poultry Processing: A Comprehensive Review of Isolate Heterogeneity, Stress Adaptation, and Antimicrobial Resistance
pool.abstract: Salmonella enterica remains a major foodborne pathogen in poultry-processing environments, where its persistence is largely attributed to biofilm formation on food-contact and non-food-contact surfaces. Despite extensive research on Salmonella control, persistent contamination continues to challenge food safety due to the complex interplay among isolate-specific traits, stress adaptation, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This review critically examines the phenotypic and genotypic determinants associated with Salmonella biofilm formation and evaluates their contributions to persistence, stress adaptation, and AMR. Emerging evidence also indicates that mixed-species interactions, particularly with Pseudomonas spp., can influence biofilm architecture, stress tolerance, and the long-term persistence of Salmonella in poultry-processing environments. Particular attention is given to processing-associated stresses, including temperature fluctuations, desiccation, nutrient limitation, and sublethal sanitizer exposure, which can induce adaptive responses that enhance biofilm development, promote persistence, and increase tolerance to antimicrobial interventions. The review further evaluates current detection approaches, including viability-based quantification methods such as digital droplet PCR, and discusses their limitations and applications in identifying and quantifying biofilm-associated and viable but nonculturable (VBNC) populations within processing environments. Existing control measures are assessed with emphasis on the challenges posed by mature biofilms and adaptive resistance mechanisms. Emerging antibiofilm technologies, including enzymatic treatments, bacteriophages, and UV-LED systems, are also examined for their potential industrial implementation. By integrating current knowledge on biofilm biology, stress adaptation, and AMR, this review provides a framework for developing targeted and sustainable strategies to mitigate Salmonella persistence in poultry-processing environments.

pool.title: Nutrient legacies from elephant megacarcasses create coldspots of biodiversity and hotspots of ecosystem processes
pool.abstract: Terrestrial megafauna (animals >1,000 kg) have substantial impacts on ecosystems while alive; yet, we know little about the impacts of these ecosystem engineers after they die. Like whale carcasses in the ocean, terrestrial megacarcasses may leave ecological legacies via the nutrient pulses they create on the landscape. Here, we investigated the impact of elephant megacarcasses on savanna ecosystems in Kruger National Park, South Africa. To determine how elephant carcasses affect below- and aboveground biodiversity and ecosystem processes, we collected soil and plant samples from 40 carcass sites (pairing "on carcass" and "off carcass" samples) ranging from 8 d to 7.7 y postmortem. We found that elephant carcasses released enormous pools of nutrients into savanna soils, increasing ammonium by 31×, nitrate by 7×, and phosphorus by 3× on average. These extreme ammonium concentrations were negatively correlated with the biodiversity of bacteria and plants, which were both suppressed at elephant carcass sites. Despite these decreases in biodiversity, ecosystem processes were strongly elevated at elephant carcass sites, with soil microbial respiration elevated for 1 to 2 y and herbivore grazing >3× higher for 7+ y postmortem. These results demonstrate that elephant megacarcasses generate coldspots of biodiversity but hotspots of ecosystem processes, unveiling a cryptic ecological function of megaherbivores that is extreme in both magnitude and duration relative to carcasses of smaller animals. As humans drive terrestrial megafauna toward extinction, we risk losing not only their ecosystem engineering abilities while they are alive but also the ecological legacies their carcasses create after death.
