pool.title: PoLoCo: a reproducible pooled low-coverage workflow for draft genome assembly and allele frequency analysis from ethanol-preserved small non-model invertebrates
pool.abstract: Abstract Background Many ecologically important small invertebrates are preserved in ethanol, which compromises DNA integrity and severely limits their potential to be utilized in further genomic research. The lack of soil arthropod representation ultimately results in limited availability of reference genomes and population genomic inference from pooled sequencing (Pool-seq). Results We introduce PoLoCo (Pooled Low-Coverage), a reproducible workflow integrating pooled specimen draft genome assembly from ethanol-preserved specimens with population-level allele-frequency analysis. We assembled a 411 Mb draft genome of Entomobrya nivalis from pooled short reads, achieving 97.7% BUSCO completeness despite notable fragmentation. Comparison with the published reference genome showed partial genomic correspondence while also revealing reference-dependent differences in the retained SNP datasets. The application of PoLoCo to 82 retained pooled populations produced a final distance-thinned allele-frequency dataset suitable for population-scale genomic inference. Case-study execution documented the computational requirements of the major workflow components on standard HPC infrastructure, with the workflow, documentation, and software environments openly available in Zenodo. Conclusions PoLoCo demonstrates that draft genome assemblies and reproducible Pool-seq allele-frequency analyses can be performed with long-preserved sample material from the field. PoLoCo integrates reference construction, sync-based allele-frequency analysis, and benchmarking into a free and open workflow. It establishes a reproducibility benchmark for biodiversity genomics and yields a transferable workflow for ecological and evolutionary initiatives where high-quality DNA or long-read sequencing is not feasible.
pool.authors: Mohammad Jamil Shuvo, Gernot Segelbacher, Julia C. Geue

pool.title: A functionally divergent paralog of the tRNA splicing ligase required for cell division but not tRNA maturation in Trypanosoma brucei
pool.abstract: In eukaryotes a varying number of tRNAs undergo splicing, rendering them functional for protein synthesis; tRNA splicing is thus essential. Trypanosoma brucei ( T. brucei ) has a single intron-containing, tRNA Tyr , still requiring a fully functional splicing machinery. Splicing involves intron cleavage by the splicing-specific tRNA endonuclease complex, followed by exon ligation, which in some eukaryotes (including T. brucei ) is performed by the multi-domain enzyme tRNA Ligase (TRL1). Using phylogenetic comparative analysis, we and others showed the existence of a paralog of TbTRL1, which lacks the conserved ligase residues but maintains apparently intact kinase and phosphodiesterase domains. Here, we demonstrate that down regulation of the paralogous protein (we termed TbKCPD) by RNAi causes a growth defect, which cannot be rescued by providing a spliced version of tRNA Tyr . We also tested the functionality of the kinase and phosphodiesterase domains by genetic rescue with a recoded copy of the gene impervious to RNAi. We show that both domains are essential for viability. Global proteomics comparing RNAi induced to control cells unexpectedly revealed effects on proteins primarily involved in flagellar biogenesis and in line with this observation, we also show that TbKCPD leads to defects in cell division; an essential function that goes beyond splicing.
pool.authors: Ananth Casius, Bankatesh Kumar, Gabriel Silveira d’Almeida, Christopher L. de Graffenried, Zdeněk Paris, Juan D. Alfonzo

pool.title: Progress in D rug - R elease C haracteristics and A pplications of B iodegradable D rug - L oaded H ydrogels
pool.abstract: Biodegradable drug‑loaded hydrogels possess high water content, excellent biocompatibility and in‑situ formability, which enables them to achieve localized targeted drug delivery. Thanks to these outstanding material properties, they have become core biomaterials supporting precise regional drug delivery in biomedical practice. These hydrogels have gone through noticeable functional evolution and are no longer simple passive‑diffusion‑based carriers; instead, they have developed into intelligent therapeutic platforms capable of adapting to tissue microenvironments. This paper systematically sorts out the core regulatory mechanisms behind drug release of biodegradable drug‑loaded hydrogels, and analyzes how intrinsic material properties and in‑vivo physiological environments affect drug‑release behaviors from four dimensions: cross‑linking structure, pore structure, pH responsiveness, and temperature responsiveness. This review further sorts out application progress of such hydrogels across four typical clinical scenarios, including cutaneous wound repair, local myocardial infarction treatment, interventional targeted tumor therapy, and bone‑defect regeneration. It also summarizes key industrial bottlenecks hindering their clinical translation, such as insufficient suppression of burst drug release, high technical barriers for fabricating integrated multifunctional hydrogels, as well as translational difficulties in large‑scale production and clinical approval. At the same time, this paper puts forward several key directions for follow‑up research, covering multi‑stimuli‑responsive delivery systems, sequential multi‑drug co‑delivery strategies, composite hydrogels with tissue‑matching mechanical properties, and the construction of standardized in‑vivo evaluation systems. This study offers comprehensive theoretical references for structural optimization, performance improvement and clinical translation of biomedical biodegradable drug‑loaded hydrogels.
pool.authors: Yifan Mao

pool.title: Enerzyme: An Efficient Reactive Neural Network Potential Training Framework for Enzyme Cluster Models with Application to Methyltransferases
pool.abstract: Abstract Quantum mechanical (QM) cluster models provide an effective framework for mechanistic studies of enzymatic reactions but QM calculations remain computationally demanding. Neural network potentials (NNPs) offer a promising route to reduce their cost, but enzymes introduce new challenges not faced by NNPs for small molecules, including large system sizes, the need for inclusion of solvent environments, substantial polarization, and charge transfer. Here, we demonstrate an integrated software framework for efficient training of NNPs for mechanistic study of enzymes, with demonstrations on QM-cluster models of S-adenosyl-l-methionine-dependent methyltransferases (MTases). Our Enerzyme code introduces modular, electrostatics-aware NNP architectures and combines automated QM-cluster construction with reactive dataset generation. The Enerzymette subpackage also automates reaction pathway exploration at both NNP and DFT levels of theory. We show that iterative flexible scans and nudged elastic band calculations impose stricter requirements on NNPs than conventionally employed dataset metrics. Nevertheless, we develop an approach to train NNPs on fewer than 1,000 system-specific data points to reproduce reaction energetics and transition-state structures on MTase clusters containing up to 545 atoms, approaching chemical accuracy with respect to the reference. We show that direct supervision of atomic charges and alignment of dielectric screening with QM-cluster calculations substantially improve simulation stability and accuracy and that multitask-learned atomic charges predict correct charge transfer and polarization trends and provide chemically meaningful descriptors of reactivity. Furthermore, we demonstrate transferability across chemically diverse catechol O-methyltransferase substrates, indicating NNPs learn generalizable reactivity patterns as training data is expanded across multiple enzymes. Together, these results establish a foundation for accelerating enzyme mechanistic studies and provide insights for future NNP development for biomolecular reactivity.
pool.authors: Weiliang Luo, Heather J. Kulik

pool.title: Cyclophilin D deficiency exacerbates diet-induced obesity and selectively enhances skeletal muscle mitochondrial respiration in male mice
pool.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity-associated metabolic disease, with the mitochondrial permeability transition pore serving as a key regulator of cellular energy homeostasis. Cyclophilin D, encoded by Ppif, is the principal regulatory component of this pore and has been implicated in insulin secretion, adipocyte survival, and whole-body energy balance. However, whether Ppif loss produces a consistent metabolic phenotype when challenged with high fat diet (HFD) exposure, and whether systemic metabolic alterations reflect tissue-specific changes in mitochondrial oxidative capacity, remains unresolved. Here, we characterized male, 21-weeks-old mice with germline Ppif deletion longitudinally over 34 weeks under standard (SD) and HFD using body composition analysis, indirect calorimetry, glucose and insulin tolerance testing and tissue-resolved, Seahorse-based mitochondrial respirometry. Under SD, knockout mice displayed elevated fat mass without differences in food intake or energy expenditure. High-fat feeding progressively amplified this adiposity, with knockout mice developing significantly greater body weight and fat mass than wild-type littermates by weeks 28 and 36. Glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity remained comparable between genotypes under either diet. ANCOVA revealed significant effects of lean mass (p < 0.001) and genotype (p = 0.017) on energy expenditure, as well as a significant lean mass × genotype interaction (p = 0.025). Consistent with a distinct contribution of lean mass to EE in KO vs. WT mice, we found increased ADP-stimulated mitochondrial respiration in quadriceps of knockout mice under both diets, without corresponding differences in brown adipose tissue or liver, or changes in mitochondrial content across tissues. These findings establish cyclophilin D as a diet- and tissue-specific regulator of energy homeostasis, informing therapeutic strategies targeting the permeability transition pore or cyclophilin D interactome in metabolic disease.

pool.title: The potential role of high mobility group box 1 (HMGB-1) protein in the pathogenesis of keratoconus: a pilot immunofluorescence study
pool.abstract: Aim: This preliminary study aims to evaluate the expression of high mobility group box 1 (HMGB-1) in keratoconic corneas, normal corneas, and corneas from donors with Fuchs’ corneal dystrophy using immunohistochemistry. Methods: Under a Loyola University Institutional Review Board (IRB) approved protocol (LU#219768), archived paraffin-embedded corneal tissues were obtained from the Loyola University Medical Center Department of Pathology. The study included three keratoconic corneas, three normal donor corneas, and three Fuchs’ dystrophy corneas. Tissue sections were deparaffinized in 100% xylene, rehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and subjected to antigen retrieval. Sections were stained with an HMGB-1 primary antibody, followed by a fluorescently conjugated anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody and 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) nuclear counterstain. Immunofluorescence imaging and deconvolution analysis were performed using a Nikon Eclipse Ti2 microscope equipped with a digital camera. Two prespecified comparisons, keratoconus versus normal and Fuchs’ dystrophy versus normal, were evaluated using Welch’s independent-samples t tests with Holm adjustment for multiple testing. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Results: HMGB-1 expression was increased in corneal tissues from patients with keratoconus and Fuchs’ corneal dystrophy compared with normal controls. The increased levels of HMGB-1 suggest enhanced activation of pro-inflammatory and tissue-remodeling pathways. Increased HMGB-1 expression in keratoconus may be associated with cellular stress, inflammation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Conclusions: These preliminary findings suggest that HMGB-1 expression may be increased in keratoconus; however, due to the small sample size of n = 3 per group, larger studies are needed to confirm this association and clarify its potential role in disease pathogenesis. These findings suggest that HMGB-1 may be associated with corneal cellular stress and inflammatory signaling present in keratoconic corneas and warrant further investigation and validation.

pool.title: Dock2 deficiency compromises erythroid differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells

pool.title: Decreased expression of Acsm2 disrupts energy metabolism and affects cell death in acute kidney injury
pool.abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a clinical syndrome characterized by high morbidity and a significant risk of mortality. Early diagnosis of AKI provides a crucial therapeutic window for treatment. There is an urgent need for universal biomarkers for the early diagnosis of AKI. Methods We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of AKI and found that Acsm2 was downregulated in the S1, S2, and S3 segments in AKI. Differential analysis, enrichment analysis, and pseudotime trajectory analysis were performed, in conjunction with animal experiments and transcriptome datasets, to explore the expression pattern and role of Acsm2 in AKI. Results Our study found that Acsm2 was significantly downregulated in the S1, S2, and S3 segments of renal tubules during the early stages of AKI. Acsm2 expression was correlated with key metabolic pathways, including fatty acid metabolism and mitochondrial function. The downregulation of Acsm2 in AKI was associated with disrupted energy metabolism and increased cell death, including apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis in proximal tubular cells (PTCs). Conclusion Downregulation of Acsm2 in AKI is correlated with impaired energy metabolism and cell death in PTCs, suggesting that Acsm2 may serve as a potential biomarker for the early diagnosis and intervention of AKI. Further studies on its mechanistic role could provide new insights into the pathophysiology of AKI and offer novel therapeutic strategies.
pool.authors: Binyu Wang, Yan Zha

pool.title: Potential role of irisin-mediated oxidative stress defense in systemic diseases
pool.abstract: Oxidative stress arises when excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) overwhelm endogenous antioxidant defenses, leading to deleterious modifications of lipids, proteins, and DNA. Persistent oxidative stress is implicated in the pathogenesis of numerous chronic disorders, including cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative conditions, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and ischaemia–reperfusion (I/R) injury across multiple organs. Irisin, a myokine/adipokine proteolytically cleaved from fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5), was first characterized in 2012. Preclinical studies have increasingly demonstrated that irisin possesses potent antioxidant properties and exerts cytoprotective effects in diverse tissues. These antioxidant actions are mediated through multiple molecular mechanisms: activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway with subsequent upregulation of cytoprotective enzymes such as haem oxygenase-1 (HO-1); sirtuin 3 (SIRT3)-dependent deacetylation and activation of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2); inhibition of pro-oxidant enzymes including NADPH oxidase (NOX); and modulation of mitochondrial fusion-fission dynamics to preserve mitochondrial homeostasis. Functionally, irisin initiates intracellular signalling cascades, including AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), PI3K/Akt, and MAPK pathways, primarily through binding to cell-surface integrin αV receptors. This review systematically summarizes the molecular mechanisms underlying irisin-mediated antioxidation, delineates its organ-protective roles in cardiovascular, neurological, metabolic, hepatic, renal, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, skeletal, reproductive systems, as well as in sepsis and ageing, and discusses its translational potential as a clinical biomarker and therapeutic target for oxidative-stress-associated diseases.
pool.authors: Xue Xiao, 吴丽颖, Xiaoming Zhu, Jie Zhou

pool.title: Chromosome 6q mediated loss of LATS1 tumour suppression as a targetable mechanism of ultra-high-risk posterior fossa A ependymoma
pool.abstract: Abstract Posterior Fossa A (PFA) is the most frequent and clinically aggressive ependymoma (EPN) subgroup, with relapse typically representing a terminal event despite intensive multimodal therapy. Ultra-high-risk PFA EPNs are characterised by chromosome 6q loss (6q-) with or without chromosome 1q gain (1q +). While the molecular mechanisms driving 1q+ have been elucidated, 6q- PFA pathobiology remains poorly understood. Here, we show that loss of 6q in PFA EPN results in deletion of LATS1 (Large Tumour Suppressor Kinase 1), thereby dysregulating the Hippo signalling pathway and enhancing YAP/TEAD activity. Integrated analyses of primary and recurrent PFA EPNs, incorporating clinical, multiomic, and functional assays, were performed to define the biology and therapeutic susceptibility of 6q- PFA EPNs. Cumulative 6q loss was associated with nearly half of PFA EPN-related deaths. Copy number profiling identified the LATS1 locus as recurrently deleted across all 6q- cases, including 10/60 with partial 6q deletions. Restoration of LATS1 expression in 6q- PFA cell lines re-established protein levels and suppressed proliferation. Tumour analyses showed marked Hippo pathway disruption with elevated YAP expression and TEAD2- related transcriptional activity. TEAD2 palmitoylation inhibitor VT107, and Proteolysis Targeted Chimera (PROTAC) degrader H122, exhibited PFA 6q- selective activity in vitro. TEAD2 upregulation was further observed in a previously described undifferentiated, progenitor-like population of PFA EPN cells. In conclusion, 6q loss defines an aggressive biological subset of PFA associated with dismal outcomes. Identification of LATS1 as a recurrently lost tumour suppressor implicates Hippo pathway dysregulation as a central driver of malignancy, and we identify YAP/TEAD signalling as a potential therapeutic target.
pool.authors: Andrew M. Donson, Andrea M. Griesinger, Rebecca J. Chapman, Richard Guy Grundy, John-Paul Kilday, Vijay Ramaswamy, Jean M. Mulcahy Levy, Michael L. Kaufman, Vladimir Amani, Julia K. Sundheimer, Kristian W. Pajtler, Nicholas K. Foreman, Timothy A. Ritzmann

pool.title: Phormidolide D, a novel cytotoxic cyanobacterial macrolide: Assessing its effects on the extracellular matrix, apoptosis, and angiogenesis.
pool.abstract: Marine cyanobacteria are a rich source of structurally diverse secondary metabolites and have inspired at least four anticancer drugs currently on the market, highlighting their potential for the discovery of new therapeutic candidates. This study aimed to discover and elucidate the structure of a novel halogenated polyketide from marine cyanobacteria and to characterize its cytotoxic and mechanistic profile. Phormidolide D (1) was discovered through bioactivity-guided isolation, and its structure was elucidated using NMR and HR-MS/MS analyses. Cytotoxicity was evaluated in SH-SY5Y, HepG2, HCT 116, and hCMEC/D3 cell lines. Its biological activity was further characterized in 2D and 3D HCT 116 models by assessing spheroid morphology, extracellular matrix-related mRNA expression, combination effects with staurosporine, cell cycle distribution and apoptosis. In vivo anti-angiogenic activity was evaluated in transgenic zebrafish (Tg(fli1a:EGFP) embryos. Phormidolide D (1) exhibited potent cytotoxicity against the human colon carcinoma cell line HCT 116 in both monolayer and spheroid cultures (IC50 = 0.83 μM and 30.80 μM, respectively), whereas phormidolide A (2) was inactive. Phormidolide D (1) affected the 3D spheroid architecture, as demonstrated by fluorescence imaging. Its effects on the extracellular matrix were further observed by increased matrix metalloproteinase 1 mRNA expression and reduced collagen type I transcripts. Co-treatment of a phormidolide rich fraction with sub-effective concentrations of staurosporine reduced spheroid viability, with Bliss analysis confirming a synergistic interaction. Treatment with phormidolide D (1) increased sub-G1 cell population and early apoptotic cells. Furthermore, transgenic zebrafish embryos exposed to phormidolide D (1) had reduced vascularization, suggesting further studies for anti-angiogenic potential. These findings highlight phormidolide D (1), a structurally unique marine natural product distinguished by an unprecedented bromomethylene ketone, as a promising lead for anticancer drug development.
pool.authors: Ferreira L, Ribeiro T, Peravali R, Vasconcelos V, Urbatzka R, Reis M

pool.title: Proximity-Engineered Dual-Atomic Cobalt Sites Enable Adaptive Spin Catalysis for Simultaneous Oxygen and Peroxide Reduction.
pool.abstract: Breaking the intrinsic adsorption conflicts among oxygen intermediates remains a central challenge in oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) electrocatalysis. Although spin-state engineering offers an effective strategy for tuning catalytic activity, conventional approaches generally focus on a single-spin configuration, which cannot simultaneously satisfy the distinct energetic requirements of different ORR intermediates. Here, we introduce an adaptive spin catalysis concept through proximity engineering of dual-atomic Co sites confined within a one-dimensional covalent organic framework. Precisely regulating the Co-Co separation while preserving the local coordination environment induces inter-site electronic coupling, giving rise to coexisting high-spin and low-spin Co configurations. Combined spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations support a mechanistic framework in which these coexisting spin configurations provide complementary catalytic functions for distinct intermediates along the multistep ORR pathway, thereby alleviating adsorption conflicts. Consequently, the proximity-engineered catalyst delivers outstanding ORR activity with a half-wave potential of 0.96 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode, outperforming both its spatially separated counterpart and commercial Pt/C. The catalyst also efficiently mediates both O2 and H2O2 reduction while suppressing peroxide decomposition, enabling enhanced performance in rechargeable zinc-air batteries and peroxide-assisted aluminum-air batteries. This work establishes a molecular framework for exploiting spin-state complementarity in atomic catalysts for advanced energy-conversion reactions.
pool.authors: Cheng R, Lin X, Song J, Luo Y, Zhan Z, Cai S, Fu C, Vlad A, Li G

pool.title: Scalable low-thermal-budget fabrication of suspended silicon nanowire devices
pool.abstract: Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) are versatile one-dimensional building blocks for gas and biochemical sensors, MEMS/NEMS physical transduction platforms, and integrated electronic devices because of their high surface-to-volume ratios and compatibility with semiconductor processing. A key limitation of conventional top-down fabrication is its reliance on furnace-based high-temperature steps, such as thermal oxidation and LPCVD, which can induce residual stress and constrain post-CMOS integration because of thermal-budget limits above 400 °C. Here, we present a furnace-free, low-thermal-budget fabrication approach for suspended Si NWs with a maximum process temperature of 180 °C. The process forms suspended Si NWs at the top surface of both bulk Si substrates and SOI substrates with a 2 µm device layer. The method defines a nanoscale Si surface protrusion and uses a conformal Cr sidewall coating to preserve linewidth during DRIE release. The process yields suspended Si NWs with critical dimensions down to 50 nm, aspect ratios of up to 100, and array pitches of 5 µm, while supporting integration into junctionless field-effect transistor architectures. Electrical measurements confirm ohmic behavior in two-terminal NW devices and demonstrate depletion-mode current modulation in side-gated junctionless FETs, with a threshold voltage of 24 V and approximately 40× current modulation. After nominal 2 nm Pd functionalization, single-NW devices exhibit repeatable 1% H 2 sensing, producing near-complete current suppression of the p-type NW channel at sub-10 nW operating power. By eliminating furnace-based processing, the approach supports post-CMOS-compatible integration, avoids high-temperature stress-inducing process steps, and establishes a scalable platform for suspended Si NW devices.
pool.authors: Basit Ali, Arda Deniz Yalcinkaya, Çağrı Arslan, Umut Kerimzade, B. Erdem Alaca

pool.title: Ulvan, carrageenan, and fucoidan: comparative immunomodulatory mechanisms and future directions in major algal sulfated polysaccharides
pool.abstract: Sulfated polysaccharides derived from marine algae have attracted considerable interest in innate immunity research due to their structural diversity and pronounced immunomodulatory activities. Ulvan, carrageenan, and fucoidan, derived from green, red, and brown algae, respectively, represent three paradigmatic classes of algal sulfated polysaccharides. This review establishes a four-tier analytical framework, namely “structural features, receptor recognition, signaling pathways, and immune outcomes”, to systematically compare their mechanistic differences in innate immune modulation. This framework provides, for the first time, a unified causal chain from molecular structure to immune effector phenotypes. Ulvan is characterized by coordinated TLR4/cGAS-STING dual pathways: it drives pro-inflammatory responses via the TLR4-MyD88-NF-κB axis while inducing type I interferon production through the cGAS-STING-TBK1-IRF3 cascade. TBK1, as a shared downstream node of both the TLR4-TRIF and cGAS-STING pathways, may mediate signal integration and amplification, thereby conferring a distinctive advantage to ulvan in antiviral immunity. Carrageenan exhibits dual TLR4/NLRP3 activities, with κ/ι/λ subtypes displaying a functional spectrum from localized pro-inflammation to systemic immunostimulation, determined by their sulfate content and gelation properties. A critical distinction must be made between high-molecular-weight native carrageenan (>100 kDa), which is minimally absorbed in the intestine and considered safe, and low-molecular-weight degraded carrageenan (<50 kDa), which carries inflammatory and toxic risks. Fucoidan achieves immunomodulatory pleiotropy through dual TLR4/CLR recognition and concurrent engagement of multiple signaling cascades, encompassing NF-κB-driven pro-inflammation, bidirectional NLRP3 inflammasome regulation, and complement C3 activation. The antiviral effect of fucoidan via the STING pathway, potentially dependent on ROS-mediated DNA damage or endoplasmic reticulum stress, mechanistically differs from ulvan’s cGAS-STING activation. The structural basis driving this pathway selectivity resides in an inverse gradient relationship between sulfate and uronic acid contents across the three polysaccharides: sulfate content ranks as fucoidan > carrageenan > ulvan, while uronic acid content follows the opposite order. This inverse gradient serves as the first unified structural principle explaining differential receptor preferences and pathway selection among these three distinct classes of algal polysaccharides. Based on this framework, we propose differentiated polysaccharide design strategies tailored to three therapeutic objectives (pro-inflammation, antiviral defense, and immune balance), offering a roadmap for structure-guided immunomodulation using algal sulfated polysaccharides.

pool.title: Halogenated and metallic scaffolds as novel efflux pump inhibitors: mechanistic insight in overcoming antimicrobial and cross-domain resistance
pool.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is increasing rapidly, necessitating the development of non-traditional therapeutic approaches. Overexpression of bacterial efflux pumps mediates active extrusion of drugs and is a major mechanism underlying multidrug resistance (MDR) in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens. Inhibition of efflux pumps (EPIs) can restore the activity of conventional antibiotics that have lost efficacy due to resistance. Here, we examine two classes of non-antibiotic adjuvants: halogenated small molecules and metal-based coordination complexes or nanoparticles. Halogen bonding and related chemical modifications can modulate membrane permeability and influence binding kinetics within bacterial transporters. Metal-based antimicrobial compounds utilize specific three-dimensional geometries and iron-mimicry to disrupt microbial transport systems. Notably, although microbial efflux pumps and mammalian multidrug transporters are structurally and mechanistically distinct, they share a functional role in reducing intracellular drug accumulation. This functional convergence provides a rationale for investigating whether selected EPI scaffolds developed in antimicrobial systems may also modulate resistance-associated transport processes in cancer. However, evidence supporting such cross-domain activity remains predominantly preclinical, and functional activity in one biological system should not be interpreted as evidence of therapeutic equivalence or clinical transferability to the other. By integrating structure–activity relationships, transporter mechanisms, microenvironmental pH effects, and translational limitations, this review highlights the potential of halogenated and metal-based scaffolds as experimental EPI platforms while emphasizing the substantial pharmacological, safety, and validation challenges that remain before clinical application.
pool.authors: Manaf AlMatar, Raja Lakhal, Kamaleldin H. Kamaleldin, Arig Ibrahim-Hashim

pool.title: Plant-derived extracellular nanovesicles in musculoskeletal repair and functional rehabilitation: mitochondrial–immune–metabolic regulation
pool.abstract: Musculoskeletal injuries and degenerative disorders caused by trauma, aging, chronic inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction frequently result in impaired functional recovery, including skeletal muscle atrophy, bone loss, cartilage degeneration, and neuromuscular dysfunction. Although exercise rehabilitation, physical therapy, and pharmacological interventions can improve clinical outcomes, their ability to restore the complex pathological microenvironment characterized by persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metabolic imbalance remains limited. Plant-derived extracellular nanovesicles (PELNs), naturally occurring lipid-bilayer nanoparticles containing diverse bioactive cargos such as RNAs, proteins, lipids, and phytochemicals, have recently emerged as promising regulators of tissue repair. Unlike conventional nanoparticles that mainly serve as passive delivery carriers, PELNs possess intrinsic biological activity and can actively modulate cellular states across biological barriers. Increasing evidence indicates that PELNs contribute to musculoskeletal regeneration by regulating inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, mitochondrial homeostasis, stem/progenitor cell activity, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Recent studies have reported regenerative effects of PELNs in experimental models involving skeletal muscle, bone, and peripheral nerve tissues. Beyond tissue-specific effects, accumulating evidence suggests that PELN-mediated regeneration involves coordinated mitochondrial–immune–metabolic reprogramming, including regulation of mitochondrial quality control, inflammatory signaling, and immunometabolic states. This review summarizes recent advances in PELN-mediated musculoskeletal repair and their potential relevance to functional recovery, highlighting their biological properties, therapeutic applications, and underlying regulatory mechanisms. The challenges and future perspectives of engineered PELNs for regenerative rehabilitation are also discussed.
pool.authors: Ningning Zhu, Ningrui Wang, Nana Zhou, Baodong Ye, Jingjing Liu

pool.title: Photo-Activatable RNA Switches for Optical Control of Cell-Free Protein Synthesis
pool.abstract: Abstract Programmable RNA switches enable target-dependent regulation of cell-free protein synthesis. Here, we report a photo-activatable RNA switch using photocleavable Lock DNA (pcl-Lock) to enable optical control of in vitro translation. Synthesized by solid-phase methods, pcl-Lock incorporates a coumarin-based photocleavable linker that maintains the RNA switch in an inactive state. Irradiation with 456 nm light cleaves the linker, releasing inhibition and activating translation. Light-triggered activation produced β-galactosidase, yielding approximately 4-fold and 30-fold increases in fluorescence and glucose signals, respectively. Native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis confirms efficient photocleavage of the pcl-Lock strand, while control experiments verify that light-dependent activation does not occur with the Lock strand lacking the photocleavable linker. This strategy enables optical regulation of cell-free protein synthesis and establishes a strategy for integrating photochemical control with programmable gene regulation.
pool.authors: Natalie E. Connell, Mahla Lashkari, Emmett Hanson, Ian M. McClain, Maya Dellocono-Forstner, Maksim Royzen, Mehmet Veysel Yigit

pool.title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design
pool.abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.
pool.authors: Enes Üstüner, Mustafa Öz

pool.title: Niallia Circulans mediated Bio-fabrication of ZnO nanoparticles: Synthesis, characterization, and multifunctional applications
pool.abstract: The current study addresses increasing global problems (agricultural sustainability, environmental contamination, and antimicrobial resistance) by means of sustainable and multifunctional biosynthesized Zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs). The study utilized a cell-free supernatant of a novel endophytic bacterial strain (Niallia Circulans) to synthesize ZnO NPs. Biosynthesized NPs were evaluated by using various techniques of characterization. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was revealed by UV-Visible spectral peak for ZnO NPs at 355 nm. A X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed a crystallite size of 90.64 nm, while scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) demonstrated the predominance of hexagonal-structured zinc, carbon, and oxygen elements. The functional groups in Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) confirm the presence of biomolecules. The evaluated multifunctional application of biosynthesized ZnO NPs exhibits an enhanced early seedling growth rate and increased seed germination (100% in 12 h) on cowpea (Vigna unguiculata L.) compared to the control groups. Also shows excellent antibacterial activity against test bacterial strains. Additionally, a high removal efficiency of 97.85% was achieved within 110 min for 10 ppm methylene blue dye solution at pH 9. This study highlights the endophytic bacteria-mediated successful synthesis of ZnO NPs, with potential multifunctional applications in agriculture, antimicrobial treatments, and environmental remediation.
pool.authors: Kiran Prasad, Bhakti R. Patel, Gautam V. Priyadarshi, Dinesh Bhatia, Rakesh Kumar Verma, Esha Rami, Dipak Kumar Sahoo, Snehal Bagatharia, Ashish Patel

pool.title: Mitigating zoonotic pathogens in the food supply chain: veterinary strategies and biosensor technologies for ensuring the safety of animal-derived products
pool.abstract: Zoonotic diseases, which are transmitted from animals to humans, represent a major global public health concern, particularly through the consumption of contaminated animal-derived food products such as meat, dairy, eggs, and seafood. These foods, while nutritionally essential, can act as carriers of pathogenic microorganisms, such as Brucella , Listeria , Campylobacter , and Salmonella . This review explores the risk of zoonotic pathogens in the food supply chain and presents an integrated approach to control contamination at various stages of food production and distribution. Key strategies include pre-harvest controls on farms, such as improved husbandry, vaccination, and biosecurity measures; post-harvest interventions aimed at reducing microbial contamination during slaughter, processing, storage, and transport; and the promotion of hygienic food handling and distribution practices. At the consumer level, education and awareness campaigns play a critical role in reducing foodborne infections. Furthermore, continuous monitoring through veterinary inspections and pathogen surveillance enables early detection of and response to outbreaks. The adoption of food safety standards, regulatory frameworks, and advanced traceability systems, enhanced by biosensor technologies, further strengthens food safety management. These coordinated efforts are essential for ensuring the safety of animal-derived foods, preventing zoonotic disease transmission, and safeguarding public health.
pool.authors: Xiaohui Liang, Chang Xu, Tingting Sun, Sijia Lu, Kun Li, Lizeng Peng

pool.title: Curvularia lunata as a versatile pathogen causing leaf spot diseases in diverse plant species and its management strategies
pool.abstract: Curvularia lunata poses a significant threat to agricultural ecosystems worldwide, causing substantial yield losses and economic consequences across a variety of crops. As a prominent phytopathogenic fungus known for its affinity for leaf spot diseases, its proliferation warrants attention due to its remarkable adaptability and expanding influence. It can serve as a beneficial endophyte for certain plants; however, its pathogenic nature underscores its potential to affect both plant and human health. This review explores key characteristics of C. lunata , including its morphology characterized by dark, velvety colonies and distinctive crescent-shaped spores. Its ecological role as a plant pathogen is examined, emphasizing the damage it can inflict on crops. Additionally, C. lunata is known to produce various secondary metabolites, including phytotoxic and other biologically active compounds. Collectively, current evidence identifies C. lunata as a biologically versatile and epidemiologically important pathogen whose effective management depends on accurate identification, understanding of host–pathogen interactions, and recognition of environmental conditions that favor disease development. No single control approach is consistently sufficient across pathosystems; rather, sustainable management requires the integration of cultural, biological, and judicious chemical measures according to host and production conditions. This synthesis therefore provides a practical evidence base for disease diagnosis, risk assessment, and management decision-making by researchers and crop-protection stakeholders.
pool.authors: M. Qaisar, Muhammad Sarmad Atiq, Abdul Mubeen Lodhi, Azeem Akram, Muhammad Usman, Ghalib Ayaz Kachelo, Nasar-ur-Rehman Khan, Nawaz Ahmad, Muhammad Luqman Aleem, Nasir Ahmed Rajput

pool.title: Biofilm‐Mediated Persistence of Salmonella in Poultry Processing: A Comprehensive Review of Isolate Heterogeneity, Stress Adaptation, and Antimicrobial Resistance
pool.abstract: Salmonella enterica remains a major foodborne pathogen in poultry-processing environments, where its persistence is largely attributed to biofilm formation on food-contact and non-food-contact surfaces. Despite extensive research on Salmonella control, persistent contamination continues to challenge food safety due to the complex interplay among isolate-specific traits, stress adaptation, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This review critically examines the phenotypic and genotypic determinants associated with Salmonella biofilm formation and evaluates their contributions to persistence, stress adaptation, and AMR. Emerging evidence also indicates that mixed-species interactions, particularly with Pseudomonas spp., can influence biofilm architecture, stress tolerance, and the long-term persistence of Salmonella in poultry-processing environments. Particular attention is given to processing-associated stresses, including temperature fluctuations, desiccation, nutrient limitation, and sublethal sanitizer exposure, which can induce adaptive responses that enhance biofilm development, promote persistence, and increase tolerance to antimicrobial interventions. The review further evaluates current detection approaches, including viability-based quantification methods such as digital droplet PCR, and discusses their limitations and applications in identifying and quantifying biofilm-associated and viable but nonculturable (VBNC) populations within processing environments. Existing control measures are assessed with emphasis on the challenges posed by mature biofilms and adaptive resistance mechanisms. Emerging antibiofilm technologies, including enzymatic treatments, bacteriophages, and UV-LED systems, are also examined for their potential industrial implementation. By integrating current knowledge on biofilm biology, stress adaptation, and AMR, this review provides a framework for developing targeted and sustainable strategies to mitigate Salmonella persistence in poultry-processing environments.
pool.authors: Md Anamul Hasan Chowdhury, Chowdhury Sanat Anjum Reem, Md. Furkanur Rahaman Mizan, Md. Ashrafudoulla, Sang‐Do Ha

pool.title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation
pool.abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid 1 H- 15 N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.
pool.authors: Chung-Ta Han, Karen Tsay, Samuel Lobo, Saeed Najafi, Kieran Monahan, Erica Hong, M. Scott Shell, Joan‐Emma Shea, Songi Han

pool.title: Manufacturing Route-Dependent Biointerface Modulation in 3D-Printed and Conventional Dental Implant Systems
pool.abstract: Implant manufacturing routes determine surface architecture and, consequently, modulate biointerface interactions that govern early biological responses. Although additive manufacturing has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional subtractive techniques, direct comparisons among commercially available systems remain limited. In this study, a commercially available additively manufactured dental implant was compared with four market-available conventionally machined systems to elucidate manufacturing route-dependent biointerface modulation. Physicochemical properties, surface topography, and electrochemical behavior were evaluated alongside biological responses. Protein adsorption profiles were characterized by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), while polymicrobial accumulation was quantified and profiled. Microbially induced surface degradation was assessed by titanium ion release. The additively manufactured implant and the market-leading conventional system exhibited higher surface roughness and distinctive topographical features, which were associated with reduced polymicrobial biofilm accumulation, lower titanium ion release following microbial challenge, and stable electrochemical behavior. Although conventionally machined implants exhibited broader proteomic profiles, functional enrichment analyses revealed overlapping biological categories among implant systems. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that the manufacturing route critically modulates implant biointerface characteristics, with additive manufacturing achieving performance comparable to established commercial systems.

pool.title: Water quality monitoring challenges during the war in Ukraine: new contaminants and approaches to their detection
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT Graphical overview of water pollution and monitoring under conflict conditions. Water pollutants are grouped into conflict-related contaminants, including explosive compounds, ammunition additives, uranium and heavy metals; conventional pollutants, including nutrients, heavy metals and organic matter; and hazardous pollutants also occurring in civilian activities, including petroleum hydrocarbons, pesticides, phenols, pharmaceuticals, personal care products and microplastics. A hybrid monitoring concept combines laboratory ex situ analysis, field in situ measurements and remote monitoring. These monitoring approaches are supported by a four-level digital framework consisting of sensor networks, analytics and Big Data, decision support, and an integrative level. The article provides a critical assessment of the ability of routine water quality monitoring systems to operate under armed conflict conditions, using Ukraine as a case study. Conventional pollutants (metals, nutrients, organic contamination, and emerging environmental threats, including pharmaceuticals and microplastics), are provided. Particular attention is paid to substances that are specific to wartime conditions, including explosive compounds, fuel and lubricant components, and metals derived from munitions. It is shown that infrastructure damage, electricity shortages, restricted access to monitoring sites, and disruption of laboratory operations can distort results or fully halt classical ex situ monitoring, creating spatial and temporal data gaps. Against conflict specific requirements, including personnel safety, rapid diagnostics, and data continuity, the performance of laboratory, in situ, and remote sensing approaches are evaluated. The analysis supports implementation of hybrid monitoring architectures that combine satellite Earth observation, use of UAVs for sampling or reconnaissance, and mobile laboratories for confirmatory analysis, complemented by portable test systems for rapid screening. Priorities for digitalization of crisis monitoring are formulated, including deployment of IoT based sensors, data standardization, and development of a Big Data platform with an interactive map to support early warning systems and post war recovery planning.
pool.authors: Світлана Олександрівна Кирій, Khrystyna Hutsul, Arcady Shakhnovsky, Iryna V. Kosogina, Марта Ігорівна Літинська, Tetiana A. Dontsova

pool.title: Svep1 orchestrates distal airway patterning and alveolar differentiation in murine lung development
pool.abstract: Abstract Disruptions in airway branching or alveolar differentiation during lung development can lead to severe respiratory deficiencies and neonatal death. The molecular mechanisms governing branching patterning and early alveolar formation remain elusive. Loss of Svep1 function in mice results in various developmental defects, including lung hypoplasia and perinatal lethality. Our examination of the lungs of Svep1 knockout ( Svep1 -/- ) mouse embryos, both in vivo and in vitro , revealed that Svep1 mutants exhibit an increase in the number of disorganized distal airway tips and progressively greater disruption of lung lobe morphology over time and saccular development. Svep1 interacts with FGF signaling to regulate smooth muscle differentiation and, together with Fgf9, guides airway branching patterning. Transcriptomic data from the lungs of Svep1 -/- embryos revealed dysregulated gene expression affecting saccular maturation. Our findings demonstrate that Svep1 is a key extracellular matrix player shaping airway morphology and influencing alveolar fate. These insights offer potential avenues for therapeutic interventions in congenital lung disorders.
pool.authors: Nicole Foxworth, Julie M. Wells, Sara Ocaña-Lopez, Sandrine Muller, Pooja Bhayani, James M. Denegre, K Palmer, Wendy Memishian, T McGee, Stephen A. Murray, Patricia K Donahoe, Carol J. Bult, M Loscertales

pool.title: Evaluation of inflammatory status and macrophage polarization in premature ovarian insufficiency mice induced by chemotherapy
pool.abstract: Background With an increasing trend of cancer occurring in young women, chemotherapy, a commonly used anticancer method, often leads to premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and infertility. Until now, there has been, however, no available treatment to cure POI patients caused by chemotherapy. This highlights the urgent need to unravel the mechanism underlying chemotherapy-induced POI development. Methods The POI mouse model was established with cyclophosphamide and busulfan. The levels of key pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines in ovaries were determined using qPCR or immunohistochemistry (IHC), while the levels of other pro-inflammatory cytokines in the serum were measured by ELISA. The macrophages (MΦs) populations and polarization within ovaries were analyzed using flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Results Initially, chemotherapy-treated mice exhibited ovarian dysfunction and a decline in ovarian reserve, characterized by disrupted hormone levels and follicular loss. Following chemotherapy, there was an increase of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including Il1b , Il6 and Tnfa in mouse ovaries. Similarly, a significant elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-18 was observed in the serum of chemotherapy-induced POI mice. Moreover, we found that the proportion of CD11c + M1-like MΦs was remarkably increased in ovaries of chemotherapy-induced POI mice compared to the controls. However, the proportion of CD206 + M2-like MΦs did not differ significantly between POI and control groups. Notably, ovarian MΦs exhibited differential distribution after chemotherapy. CD11c + M1-like MΦs mainly localized around atretic follicles, while CD206 + M2-like MΦs predominantly accumulated in ovarian stroma, accompanied by increased fibrosis. However, the Pearson analysis revealed that within the POI group, there was no significant correlation among fibrosis area, CD206 + M2-like MΦs density and the levels of key pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α) in ovaries. Conclusions Our descriptive study indicates that exacerbated inflammation and stromal fibrosis, as well as increased CD11c + M1-like MΦs polarization, occur in mouse ovaries during chemotherapy. Since these are associative findings, future interventional studies including MΦs depletion are required to examine whether a causal relationship exists between CD11c + M1-like MΦs and ovarian damage or between CD206 + M2-like MΦs and ovarian fibrosis in chemotherapy-induced POI. Moreover, additional functional research is necessary to determine whether modulating ovarian inflammation and M1/M2-like MΦs polarization would ameliorate chemotherapy-induced POI.
pool.authors: 唐卯星, Manzhi Zhao, Yangcheng Yao, Xiqian Zhang, Fenghua Liu

pool.title: ARID1B promotes DNA end resection via MDC1 and co-transactivation of DNA repair genes with c-MYC in small cell lung cancer
pool.abstract: Abstract AT-rich interactive domain-containing protein 1B (ARID1B) has been implicated in DNA damage repair; however, its precise molecular mechanisms and contributions to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) pathogenesis remain incompletely defined. In this study, analysis of clinical datasets revealed that ARID1B is significantly overexpressed in SCLC tissues and cell lines compared to normal lung tissues or lung adenocarcinoma counterparts. Functional studies in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that ARID1B depletion markedly impairs SCLC cell proliferation, clonogenicity, and tumor growth while accelerating apoptosis. Mechanistically, during the DNA double-strand break (DSB) response, ARID1B cooperates with the transcription factor c-MYC to co-activate the transcription of key DNA damage repair (DDR) genes, such as RNF8 and RAD51 . Concurrently, ARID1B is rapidly recruited to DSB sites, where it facilitates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) formation via end resection and promotes the recruitment of MDC1, a scaffold protein essential for early DDR signaling. Critically, ARID1B deficiency profoundly sensitizes SCLC cells to DNA-damaging agents, as evidenced by enhanced DNA damage persistence, apoptosis, and tumor growth inhibition in vitro and in vivo. Taken together, this study unveils a dual regulatory role of ARID1B in homologous recombination (HR) repair and establishes its potential as a therapeutic target to potentiate the efficacy of frontline chemotherapy in SCLC.
pool.authors: Peng Hou, Gongfeng Li, Guozhen Cao, Xinhuang Yao, Honglin Li, Jiahui Zhang, Jinghan Hua, Rui Guo, Li Xiang, Wenchu Lin

pool.title: Electroacupuncture pretreatment attenuates myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury-induced ferroptosis via the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway
pool.abstract: Introduction A major side effect of reperfusion therapy after myocardial infarction is myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury (MIRI). Electroacupuncture (EA) preconditioning has a long history of application in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases. This study aims to investigate whether EA preconditioning alleviates MIRI by regulating the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway to suppress the ferroptotic biochemical phenotype characterized by iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation. Methods Healthy male SPF rats were randomly divided into nine groups: Ctrl, Sham, MIRI, EA, RSL-3+EA, COTI-2+EA, Erastin+EA, COTI-2+Erastin+EA, and COTI-2+Pantethine+EA. Before MIRI induction, EA pretreatment was applied daily at CV4, bilateral ST36, and bilateral PC6 for 20 min (2 Hz, 1 mA) for 7 consecutive days. Pharmacological interventions were administered intraperitoneally once daily for 7 consecutive days before EA stimulation. The MIRI model was established by ligating the left anterior descending coronary artery for 30 min followed by 2 h of reperfusion. Myocardial oxidative stress, ferroptosis-related markers, myocardial injury markers, and cardiomyocyte apoptosis were assessed using corresponding commercial kits, DCFH-DA probe combined with flow cytometry, RhoNox-6 fluorescent probe, Western blot, RT-PCR, ELISA, and TUNEL staining combined with flow cytometry. Results EA preconditioning inhibited p53 expression, promoted the activation of the SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway, and thereby alleviated myocardial injury. The morphology of cardiomyocytes in EA-pretreated rats was altered, and the apoptosis rate of cardiomyocytes in these rats was also reduced. In addition, administration of Erastin (SLC7A11 inhibitor) showed effects similar to those of COTI-2 (p53 agonist) intervention, whereas pantethine (SLC7A11 agonist) reversed the effects of COTI-2, exerting anti-ferroptotic and cardioprotective effects. Discussion As a proof‑of‑concept study with limited sample size per experimental group, our findings preliminarily suggest that EA preconditioning ameliorates MIRI by suppressing the ferroptotic biochemical signature characterized by myocardial iron overload and lipid peroxidation through the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway. Further studies with larger sample sizes are still needed for validation.
pool.authors: Jing Mao, Qian-Ru Guo, Yi-Pu Luo, Cong-Fei Liu, Cao Zhen-yang, Yun-Tao Yu, Wen-Wei Wu, Xin-Yu Luan, Dan-Ning Xu, Hua Wang, Pu Chen, Song Wu

pool.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis
pool.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.
pool.authors: Tanvir Hossain, Abdullah Al Mahmud, Maisha Afrin, Sakibur Rahman, Shaheda Siddiqa Tahia, Ahmad Abdullah Mahdeen, Md. Habib Ullah Masum

pool.title: Protective Effects of Rosmarinic Acid Against Microplastic-Induced Oxidative Stress in RTgill-W1 Fish Gill Cell Culture: A Pharmacological In Vitro Study
pool.abstract: Microplastic contamination has emerged as a significant environmental threat to aquatic ecosystems, contributing to oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular toxicity in aquatic organisms.This study investigated the protective effects of rosmarinic acid (RA) against microplastic-induced cytotoxicity and oxidative stress using RTgill-W1 fish gill cells as an in vitro aquatic toxicology model.Cells were exposed to polystyrene microplastics (PS-MPs; 100 µg/mL) either alone or in combination with low-dose (25 µM) or high-dose (50 µM) RA for 24 h.Cell viability was determined using the MTT assay, while oxidative stress biomarkers including reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH), and catalase activity were evaluated.Inflammatory responses were assessed through quantitative PCR analysis of TNF-α and IL-1β expression.PS-MP exposure significantly reduced cell viability from 100.0 ± 2.4% to 52.6 ± 4.1% (p < 0.05), accompanied by marked increases in ROS production (248 ± 12%), MDA levels (6.8 ± 0.5 nmol/mg protein), TNF-α expression (4.86 ± 0.31-fold), and IL-1β expression (5.42 ± 0.40-fold).Simultaneously, antioxidant defenses were impaired, as evidenced by reductions in catalase activity (21.4 ± 1.8 U/mg protein) and GSH content (3.1 ± 0.3 µmol/g protein).Co-treatment with RA significantly attenuated these effects in a dose-dependent manner.The high-dose RA treatment restored cell viability to 88.4 ± 3.2%, reduced ROS and MDA levels to 122 ± 7% and 3.1 ± 0.3 nmol/mg protein, respectively, and increased catalase activity and GSH content to 43.7 ± 1.9 U/mg protein and 7.0 ± 0.3 µmol/g protein.Furthermore, RA markedly suppressed TNF-α and IL-1β expression to 1.42 ± 0.11-fold and 1.66 ± 0.13-fold, respectively.These findings demonstrate that RA effectively protects RTgill-W1 cells against microplastic-induced oxidative and inflammatory injury and highlight its potential as a natural pharmacological strategy for mitigating aquatic pollutant toxicity.
