pool.title: Zika virus produces two isoforms of the NS2A protein that play mutually exclusive roles in viral replication and virion assembly
pool.abstract: Zika virus (ZIKV), dengue virus, and several other orthoflaviviruses cause disease outbreaks in human and animal populations worldwide. The orthoflaviviral nonstructural protein 2A (NS2A) is critical for both viral replication and virion assembly. However, due to its small size, hydrophobicity, and the absence of structural information or protein-specific antibodies, we lack a clear understanding of how NS2A participates in these disparate processes. Here, using endogenously tagged NS2A-containing viral RNAs, we reveal that two NS2A isoforms are present during ZIKV infection, including both full-length NS2A and a C-terminally truncated isoform, termed NS2Aα. Phylogenetic and conservation analyses combined with polyprotein cleavage assays suggest that both NS2A isoforms are generated via the viral protease and are conserved across the Orthoflavivirus genus. Finally, using assays for viral replication and infectious particle production, we demonstrate that the two distinct NS2A isoforms function at different stages of the viral life cycle, with full-length NS2A required for viral RNA replication and NS2Aα important for virion assembly. Taken together, our data helps shed light on the form(s) and function(s) of the NS2A protein and suggests that each NS2A isoform plays a mutually exclusive role in the orthoflaviviral life cycle.
pool.authors: Breanna N. Landry, Olivia J. Klann, Hannah C.H. Hauch, Cheyanne L Bemis, Jonathan E Owen, J Harris, Trisha R. Barnard, Christopher John Neufeldt, Selena M. Sagan

pool.title: Progress in pain mechanisms and management
pool.abstract: Pain is a multifaceted sensory and emotional experience that profoundly affects human health and quality of life. It functions as a double-edged sword: while acute pain serves as a protective warning signal, chronic pain compromises physiological and psychological well-being. Pain is now widely regarded as the "fifth vital sign," and given its rising prevalence and substantial global burden, chronic pain may also be considered a major chronic disease entity. Accordingly, elucidating the neural and molecular underpinnings of pain and developing effective analgesic strategies remain urgent priorities. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular and neural circuit mechanisms that govern pain. At the molecular level, ion channels, diverse receptor systems, and intricate signaling pathways play central roles in the transduction and modulation of nociceptive signals. At the circuit level, pain processing involves ascending pathways, descending modulatory systems, and distributed brain regions that collectively encode the sensory and affective dimensions of pain. Building on these mechanistic insights, we discuss current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions, as well as emerging approaches such as gene therapy, stem cell-based therapies and neuromodulation. Despite notable progress, several challenges remain, including the adverse effects associated with existing analgesics and an incomplete understanding of visceral pain mechanisms. Future research should prioritize the integration of multiomics approaches, advanced neural circuit mapping technologies, and artificial intelligence to refine mechanistic insights and enable the development of more precise and effective pain management strategies.
pool.authors: Yongchang Li, Qian-Qian Chen, Fu‐Chao Zhang, Rui‐Xia Weng, Timothy W. Xu, Hong-Hong Zhang, Rong Gao, 连莲, Rui Li, Guang‐Yin Xu

pool.title: Berberine ameliorates thioacetamide-induced liver injury in zebrafish through PPARγ signaling and restores bile acid homeostasis
pool.abstract: Ethnopharmacological Relevance Coptis chinensis Franch. (Huanglian), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb used for “heat” and “dampness” syndromes, is clinically associated with metabolic disorders such as NAFLD. Berberine (BBR), its major bioactive alkaloid, has shown metabolic benefits, though its mechanistic basis in NAFLD remains unclear. Aim of the Study To identify candidate pathways underlying the effects of BBR in NAFLD, a computational target prediction approach was employed, followed by in vivo experimental validation in a zebrafish model. Materials and Methods A thioacetamide (TAA)-induced liver injury zebrafish model was established. Hepatic lipid accumulation and histopathology were assessed by Oil Red O staining, H&E staining, and qPCR. A computational target prediction approach was employed to identify potential BBR-NAFLD overlapping targets, followed by pathway enrichment analysis and molecular docking simulations to prioritize candidate pathways. Bile acid profiles were analyzed using UHPLC-MS/MS metabolomics. The predicted PPARγ pathway was experimentally validated using the specific antagonist GW9662 and the agonist rosiglitazone. Results BBR significantly reduced hepatic steatosis and restored liver morphology. A total of 104 overlapping targets were identified, with PPAR signaling emerging as a key pathway. BBR showed stable binding to PPARγ (−7.92 kcal/mol). In vivo, BBR restored the expression of pparg, rxra, cyp7a1, cyp27a1, and cyp8b1, all of which were suppressed by TAA; these effects were reversed by GW9662, confirming PPARγ dependence. Metabolomics revealed reduced levels of 6-ketoLCA and UDCA-3S, which were partially reversed by PPARγ inhibition. Conclusion BBR alleviates TAA-induced liver injury by regulating PPARγ and bile acid homeostasis, integrating systems pharmacology and experimental validation to support the ethnopharmacological use of C. chinensis in metabolic liver disease.
pool.authors: Peng Sun, Jun Wu, Zhu Xiaoyu, Yanshuang Ren, Zhanyi Zhou, Wenjian Zhen, Yuan Ma, Xue Ding, Menghan Huang, Yuying Zhang, Wei Gong, Hao Wang

pool.title: Network pharmacology and molecular docking-based screening of phytochemicals as multitarget inhibitors of Epstein–Barr virus infection and associated malignancies
pool.abstract: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is a class I oncogenic virus implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple lymphoid and epithelial malignancies, including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and gastric carcinoma, contributing to approximately 1.5% of all human cancers worldwide. This study employed an integrated network pharmacology and molecular docking approach to identify plant-derived bioactive compounds against EBV. A library of 1,000 phytochemicals was systematically screened against two essential EBV targets as glycoprotein 42 (Gp42) and Epstein–Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1). The top 10 compounds against each protein were prioritized based on binding affinity and interaction profiling. Putative gene targets of these compounds were retrieved and intersected with EBV-related cancer-associated genes, yielding 132 common targets. Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis identified ten hub genes centrally involved in viral oncogenesis. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment revealed significant involvement in cancer signalling pathways. Hecogenin emerged as the lead computationally prioritized candidate, exhibiting the highest binding affinities against nine of the ten cancer-associated targets, with favourable hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions. ADMET profiling suggested favourable predicted safety-related properties for Hecogenin, including high gastrointestinal absorption, blood–brain barrier permeability, and absence of AMES toxicity. Hecogenin emerges from this computational analysis as a phytochemical with predicted multitarget interactions; however, these findings are preliminary, and further preclinical and experimental validation is required against EBV infection and EBV-associated malignancies. Separately, this study establishes a robust computational framework for the discovery of mechanism-based antiviral agents from natural sources.
pool.authors: Zara Javaid, Hafiza Salaha Mahrosh, Saad Serfraz, Amer Jamil

pool.title: Computational design and translational development of TCR-mimic scFv antibodies for peptide-HLA neoantigen targeting
pool.abstract: Single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) penetrate tissue more effectively than full antibodies and are simpler to produce, but the mutant proteins that define a tumor are predominantly intracellular and therefore inaccessible to conventional antibodies. What is accessible is the mutation-derived peptide displayed on cell-surface HLA. This review concerns TCR-mimic scFvs directed at those peptide-HLA complexes. It separates three questions that are frequently conflated: which mutations are predicted to be presented, which presented complexes are genuinely targetable given surface density and cross-reactivity risk, and how immunogenic the resulting therapeutic molecule will itself be. We review computational strategies spanning target identification, AI-driven structure prediction, de novo design, affinity and specificity engineering, half-life extension and deimmunization, and distinguish throughout between the scFv as a recognition module and the effector architecture, such as a CD3 bispecific, a chimeric antigen receptor binding domain or an Fc-containing format, in which it must ultimately be deployed.
pool.authors: Sarfaraz K. Niazi, Matthias Magoola, Zamara Mariam

pool.title: Proportionate evidence in biosimilar development: when a comparative efficacy study can still change the regulatory conclusion
pool.abstract: Biosimilar regulation was established using a systematic, stepwise framework in which clinical comparisons addressed residual uncertainties following comprehensive quality and pharmacokinetic assessments. Advances in analytical resolution, clinical pharmacology, and over two decades of regulatory expertise have substantially mitigated this residual uncertainty. This publication examines circumstances in which a comparative efficacy study could still influence regulatory decisions. It presents four original analyses: a quantitative comparison of the nominal resolution of selected analytical methodologies, combined with predefined equivalence criteria, within specific clinical programs that operate at disparate scales and are used solely to demonstrate respective resolution and acceptance thresholds. Additionally, an audit of publicly available regulatory outcomes identifies 100 United States 351(k)-licensed biosimilar and interchangeable products, alongside 149 authorized European biosimilars. It also classifies 16 European nonpositive initial outcomes: nine primarily driven by quality, manufacturing, or product bridging issues; two involving clinical pharmacology or overall comparability; one following a positive opinion; and four lacking sufficient public detail. Notably, no case identified a failed comparative efficacy study as the sole decisive factor, a conclusion limited by excluding programs abandoned before filing from the dataset. An analysis of participant burden estimates indicates an aggregate of more than 10,000 enrollments for programs approved through 2019. A Bayesian value of information model shows that, under a defined base case, the net benefit of such a study diminishes once prior evidence indicates that clinical similarity substantially exceeds the decision threshold. The framework continues to emphasize targeted clinical evidence relevant to unresolved mechanisms, uncharacterized local exposure, potential immune risks, or unaddressed population-specific questions.
pool.authors: Sarfaraz K. Niazi

pool.title: Upper respiratory virome signatures reflect COVID-19 severity and post-recovery shifts
pool.abstract: Introduction Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection profoundly affects the upper respiratory tract, yet the dynamics of the resident virome across different stages of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) and recovery remain poorly understood. Methods This study profiled alterations in the virome and microbiome in 143 SARS-CoV-2–positive adults, stratified by disease severity (Non-Severe, Severe, Critical), compared with 96 RT-PCR–negative controls. Nasal and oral swabs underwent targeted viral enrichment and next-generation sequencing, followed by virome profiling. Results The respiratory virome of SARS-CoV-2-positive individuals was dominated by SARS-CoV-2, with co-detected viruses such as Human Mastadenovirus C, which increased with disease severity and persisting post-recovery. Alpha diversity was highest in Non-Severe cases and declined in Severe and Critical groups, suggesting increasing disruption of the virome with disease severity. Beta diversity showed clear separation between controls and cases, and across severity levels. LEfSe identified distinct viral signatures differentiating infection status, and logistic regression of key viral taxa accurately classified Critical versus post-recovery samples (AUC = 0.91). Although the study focused on viruses, bacterial taxa including Rothia mucilaginosa and Haemophilus parahaemolyticus were also detected with severity-linked variation, highlighting viral–bacterial interactions. Longitudinal paired analysis revealed consistent post-recovery enrichment of Streptococcus-specific bacteriophages across all severity groups, suggesting restoration of Streptococcus-associated phage dynamics during convalescence. Discussion Overall, this study reveals SARS-CoV-2–associated alterations in the respiratory virome and microbiome and highlights specific microbial taxa with potential as biomarkers for disease severity and post-infection recovery.
pool.authors: Mudita Gosain, Manjeet Kaur, Daizee Talukdar, Subhash Tanwar, Pradipta Jana, Sonali Porey Karmakar, Jyoti Kumar Verma, Susmita Bakshi, Kajal Kamboj, P. S. Verma, Madhu Pareek, Sreevatsan Raghavan, Pallavi Kshetrapal, Shinjini Bhatnagar, Jayanta Bhattacharya, Pramod Kumar Garg, Nitya Wadhwa, Bhabatosh Das

pool.title: SIRT2 in metabolism, aging, and longevity
pool.abstract: SIRT2, an NAD + -dependent deacetylase, is increasingly recognized as an important regulator of cellular metabolism and aging. By deacetylating diverse substrates, SIRT2 influences glucose metabolism, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, cytoskeletal dynamics, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses, thereby contributing to cellular metabolic homeostasis and aging. Emerging evidence suggests that age-related alterations in NAD + metabolism may affect SIRT2 activity and disrupt these processes, potentially promoting metabolic dysfunction, mitochondrial impairment, cellular senescence, and chronic inflammation. In addition, the effects of SIRT2 on aging appear to be highly context- and tissue-dependent, and its precise contribution to organismal longevity remains incompletely understood. In this review, we primarily focus on the role of SIRT2 in aging and longevity through the regulation of energy metabolism, with particular emphasis on the underlying molecular mechanisms and its interactions with metabolic and stress-responsive pathways. Understanding these mechanisms and regulations may provide new insights into SIRT2 biology and potential strategies for maintaining metabolic homeostasis and promoting healthy aging, even applications in clinic practice.
pool.authors: Menghui Li, Yihuan Dong, Wen Ren, Weixia Dong, Shaoping Ji

pool.title: Immunotechnology-based toolbox for care of chronic wounds
pool.abstract: Wound healing is a complex natural process with overlapping sequences of inflammatory, proliferation, and remodeling stages. All stages involve immune cells and their secreted molecules, including macrophages, neutrophils, and cytokines. This process becomes dysregulated in chronic wounds, such as diabetic ulcers and malignant (fungating) wounds, where healing halts before it can be completed. Both generic immunomodulation and targeted immunoengineering approaches constitute a powerful toolbox to reset healing processes. This brief review first provides background on the involvement of immune system components contribute to wound healing and their dysregulation during impaired wound healing. It then discusses the current state of knowledge on immunomodulation and immunoengineering as applied to chronic wound care. The immunomodulation approach uses stem cells or extracellular vesicles to regulate inflammation and prevent cellular senescence so that tissue regeneration takes place. Immunoengineering approaches cover the use of DNA nanoparticles to aid tissue regeneration, and aptamer-antibody conjugates to control inflammation. Finally, theranostic devices which provide real-time sensing and delivery of necessary proteins and drugs to reset wound healing have been discussed.
pool.authors: Munishwar Nath Gupta, Premlata Ambre

pool.title: Enhanced electrochemically-directed oligonucleotide synthesis via porous silica thin-film for DNA data storage
pool.abstract: DNA-based data storage has emerged as a promising alternative for long-term information archiving and its implementation accelerates the development for on-chip large scale oligonucleotide synthesis. Among various technological routes, electrochemically directed synthesis offers exceptional synthesis-site density thanks to its compatibility with semiconductor microfabrication processes. Yet increasing density typically comes at the expense of reduced per-site oligonucleotide yield, compromising the practical utility of these synthesis platforms for reliable data recovery. Here we report a porous silica thin-film strategy in order to address this fundamental trade-off by substantially increasing the effective on-chip synthesis surface area while preserving spatial confinement during electrochemically generated acid-mediated deblocking. The porous thin-film, fabricated via a sacrificial templating approach, forms an interconnected high-surface-area porous network that enables efficient reagent transport and stable electrochemical control. The presented method enables an areal oligonucleotide yield of more than 1821 pmol/cm², which represents more than 11-fold enhancement compared to a planar silica substrate. Moreover, this platform achieves comparable error statistics of deletion, insertion and substitution compared to other laboratory-built DNA data writing systems. Using this platform, we demonstrated parallel synthesis of 121-nt oligonucleotides and successful encoding, writing and error-corrected recovery of digital information. These results establish a scalable strategy for high-yield on-chip DNA synthesis and provide a practical pathway towards integrated molecular data storage systems.
pool.authors: Shijia Yang, Dayin Wang, Qiaoli Liu, Xuedong Lan, Zequan Zhao, Weidong Wang, Kai Xia, Xiuli Gao, Yuan Luo, Jianlong Zhao

pool.title: Toward a Local Manipulation of DNA by Quantum Fields
pool.abstract: Abstract Hydrogen bonds are the fundamental backbone for deoxyribo-nucleic acid (DNA) stability. In this Letter we investigate a new strategy based on plasmonic cavities to perform manipulation of hydrogen bonds in DNA. The analysis is performed using state-of-the-art Quantum Electrodynamics Coupled Cluster (QED-CC) calculations. We investigate whether in the strong coupling regime modifications of the nucleotide bases’ interactions can be induced in a totally nonintrusive manner. Our strategy proposes an alternative approach to methodologies based on a collective coupling to perform optical DNA manipulation.
pool.authors: Cenci Tommaso, Riccardo Alessandro, Enrico Ronca

metadata.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters

pool.title: A literature-weighted composite index for integrating reproductive dysfunction and cancer-associated molecular features: a reproducible computational pipeline
pool.abstract: To construct a literature-weighted composite Disease Activity Index (DAI) integrating gene-expression and DNA-methylation features associated with reproductive dysfunction and cancer, and to establish a reproducible computational pipeline for calculating the index from gene-level data. A hybrid dataset comprising 120 gene-level profiles was assembled from 50 literature-derived profiles seeded from 17 peer-reviewed sources and 70 synthetically augmented profiles. For each gene, DAI was calculated deterministically from cancer- and infertility-associated Log2FC values and a literature-derived weight according to a pre-specified formula, within a general mathematical framework that additionally specifies methylation main and interaction terms. The computational pipeline was implemented to reproduce the index and characterize its distribution. K-means clustering (k = 3) with principal component analysis (PCA) was used descriptively to characterize groupings within the resulting feature space. The pipeline reproduced the pre-specified DAI calculation, and the resulting scores showed three descriptive groupings with mean DAI values of 1.62, 1.17, and 0.91. The groupings reflected variation in the standardized molecular features used to construct the index rather than independently derived biological or clinical risk categories. This study provides a transparent, literature-weighted composite index and a reproducible computational framework for integrating gene-expression and DNA-methylation features at the intersection of reproductive dysfunction and cancer. Because DAI is derived directly from its input features and the dataset includes synthetic augmentation, the present findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Independent evaluation using patient-derived molecular measurements and clinically observed outcomes is required before clinical or diagnostic interpretation.
pool.authors: Zahra Dashti

pool.title: A multifunctional Tb3+–salicylic acid hydrazide phosphor for anti-counterfeiting, forensic fingerprint visualization, and biological applications
pool.abstract: Abstract A novel terbium(III) complex, Tb(SAH) , derived from salicylic acid hydrazide ( SAH ), was successfully synthesized and fully characterized. Stoichiometric analysis confirmed a 1:2 metal-to-ligand ratio. X-ray diffraction and microscopic studies revealed a polycrystalline structure with micro- and nanodomain features. Photoluminescence investigations demonstrated intense monochromatic emissions: blue for SAH and green for Tb(SAH) , with relatively long excited-state lifetimes in dimethylformamide (DMF), solid state, and polymeric matrices (PVA (polyvinyl alcohol), PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate), and silica xerogel). An efficient ligand-to-metal energy transfer mechanism under ultraviolet (UV) excitation was confirmed, indicating a strong antenna effect responsible for enhanced luminescence. Both SAH and Tb(SAH) were successfully applied in latent fingerprint visualization, clearly resolving level I–III ridge details on diverse porous, non-porous, and multicolored substrates. Additionally, transparent luminescent security inks prepared from the compounds exhibited excellent storage stability and humidity resistance, highlighting their suitability for anti-counterfeiting applications. Biological evaluation revealed that Tb(SAH) exhibits significantly greater in vitro cytotoxicity against the hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG-2) cell line than the free ligand. Significant antioxidant activity was observed for SAH and Tb(SAH) (IC 50 = 0.38 and 0.78 μM, respectively), surpassing ascorbic acid. The Tb(SAH) complex also exhibited improved antidiabetic activity (IC 50 = 14 μg/mL) compared with SAH (IC 50 = 44 μg/mL), with potency comparable to that of acarbose (IC 50 = 35 μg/mL). Antimicrobial studies indicated marked enhancement upon Tb 3 ⁺ coordination, particularly against Staphylococcus aureus . Molecular docking against DNA gyrase B (PDB ID: 6TCK) supported strong binding interactions, corroborating the experimental antimicrobial findings.
pool.authors: H. Nasser, Ebtesam M. Abdelrhman, M. Saif, R. Kamal, Magdy Shebl, R. Fouad

pool.title: Metabolic sensing in 3D models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: probing pH, oxygen, and lactate dynamics to decode chemoresistance
pool.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest malignancies due to its late diagnosis, extensive desmoplasia, and strong chemoresistance. Recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) in vitro modelling have provided new insights into tumor-stroma interactions and metabolic adaptations that drive disease progression. This review summarizes the pathogenesis and tumor microenvironment (TME) hallmarks of PDAC, emphasizing the metabolic heterogeneity characterized by altered pH, oxygen, and lactate gradients. It discusses conventional and emerging therapeutic strategies, the molecular basis of drug resistance, and the role of the TME in treatment failure. Furthermore, it highlights the evolution of 3D experimental models as physiologically relevant tools to study PDAC biology and evaluate drug efficacy. Special attention is given to the integration of optical biosensors for non-invasive spatio-temporal monitoring of pH and metabolic fluctuations. These sensing technologies, coupled with advanced bioengineered models, are paving the way for precision oncology and patient-tailored strategies in pancreatic cancer.
pool.authors: Anna Chiara Siciliano, Stefania Forciniti, Helena Iuele, Federica Carnevali, Giuseppe Gigli, Loretta L. del Mercato

pool.title: Development of a Chitosan-Based Nanoemulsion for Mitigating Microplastic-Induced Cytotoxicity and Oxidative Stress in RTgillW1 Fish Gill Cells
pool.abstract: Microplastic pollution is an emerging environmental concern that induces oxidative stress, inflammation, and cellular injury in aquatic organisms.Despite increasing evidence of microplastic toxicity, effective mitigation strategies remain limited.This study investigated the protective effects of a chitosan-based nanoemulsion (CS-NE) against polystyrene microplastic (PS-MP)-induced cytotoxicity and oxidative stress in RTgill-W1 fish gill cells.Chitosan nanoemulsions were prepared using ionic gelation-emulsification assisted by ultrasonication and characterized by particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta potential analyses.RTgill-W1 cells were exposed to PS-MPs (100 µg/mL) alone or in combination with low-dose (50 µg/mL) or high-dose (100 µg/mL) CS-NE for 24 h.Cell viability, oxidative stress biomarkers, and inflammatory gene expression were evaluated.The developed nanoemulsion exhibited a mean particle size of 118.6 ± 4.3 nm, a PDI of 0.21 ± 0.02, and a zeta potential of +34.8 ± 2.1 mV, indicating good colloidal stability.High-dose CS-NE showed significantly greater microplastic-binding efficiency (78.5 ± 3.2%) than the lowdose formulation (52.8 ± 2.7%).Exposure to PS-MPs reduced cell viability from 100.0 ± 2.8% to 49.2 ± 3.6%, whereas high-dose CS-NE restored viability to 91.6 ± 3.4%.PS-MPs significantly increased reactive oxygen species (276 ± 14%) and malondialdehyde levels (7.4 ± 0.6 nmol/mg protein), while reducing catalase activity and glutathione content.Co-treatment with high-dose CS-NE markedly reduced ROS (116 ± 8%) and MDA (2.8 ± 0.3 nmol/mg protein) while restoring catalase (46.2 ± 2.3 U/mg protein) and GSH (7.5 ± 0.4 µmol/g protein) levels.Furthermore, CS-NE suppressed TNF-α (1.32 ± 0.12-fold) and IL-1β (1.48 ± 0.13-fold) expression and enhanced Nrf2 expression (1.21 ± 0.09-fold).These findings demonstrate that chitosan-based nanoemulsions mitigate microplastic-induced cellular injury through microplastic sequestration and modulation of oxidative stress and inflammatory pathways, highlighting their potential as a novel nanotechnological intervention for aquatic environmental protection.

metadata.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

pool.title: A review of synthesis, characterizations, and biological activity of amphiphilic copolymers containing pendant phosphorylcholine groups
pool.abstract: Pendant 2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl phosphorylcholine (MPC) is a hydrophilic, biocompatible nanodrug, those are required for the preparation of patient-specific nanomedicine to enhance therapeutic efficacy in the human body. MPC combined with hydrophobic n -butyl methacrylate (BMA) or n -dodecyl methacrylate (DMA) with varying molecular weights and compositions obtained block (PMPC n -b-PBMA m and PMPC n -b-PDMA m ; m and n represent degrees of polymerization) and random (P(MPC/BMAx) and P(MPC/DMAx); x represents composition) copolymers with reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) radical polymerization. Their aggregation properties were evaluated by 1 H NMR spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, static light scattering (SLS), dynamic light scattering (DLS), surface tension, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and in vitro anticancer activities. The 1 H NMR data of PMPC n -b-PBMA m confirmed highly restricted motion of the n -butyl moiety through hydrophobic interactions between PMPC and PBMA blocks and established the restricted mobility of DMA and MPC pendant groups of P(MPC/DMA x ), while MPC units were trapped in a hydrophobic micro domain. Hydrophobic probe pyrene was encapsulated in PMPC n -b-PBMA m micelles to exhibit fluorescence activity. Aggregation number increased with increasing ‘x’ due to the enhancement of hydrophobic interactions between n -dodecyl groups. SLS studies can exhibit structural properties of copolymer micelles by comprising a PBMA core with a PMPC shell. DLS studies demonstrated sizes of PMPC n -b-PBMA m micelles were gradually increased with increasing PBMA block lengths. Size, surface morphology, and thickness of bilayers were confirmed by SEM and TEM. Both copolymers are used as emerging candidates in biomedical research fields because the paclitaxel drug is incorporated in micelles; that’s why PMPC forms a biocompatible outer shell to exhibit stimuli-responsive drug efficacy and gene therapy.
pool.authors: Manas Barai

pool.title: Ribonuclease H1 Hijacking: Oncotherapeutics through MicroRNA-Triggered Intracellular Construction of Long DNA/RNA Heteroduplexes
pool.abstract: Abstract Ribonuclease H1 (RNase H1) cleaves the RNA strand of DNA/RNA heteroduplexes and plays essential roles in R-loop resolution, mitochondrial DNA replication, and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) activity. Because RNase H1 has also been implicated in ASO-induced cytotoxicity, considerable effort has been focused on minimizing its activation. Here we present a reverse strategy that harnesses RNase H1-mediated cytotoxicity for cancer therapy using an oncogenic microRNA (miR-21) as an intracellular trigger. A designed hairpin DNA/hairpin RNA pair undergoes a hybridization chain reaction to assemble long-nicked DNA/RNA heteroduplexes selectively in miR-21-overexpressing cells. The resulting heteroduplexes induce RNase H1-dependent cytotoxicity in cancer cells while exhibiting minimal effects on normal cells. Treatment also caused redistribution of the paraspeckle protein P54nrb from the nucleoplasm to the nucleoli, consistent with RNase-H1-associated nucleolar stress. Furthermore, lipid-nanoparticle-mediated delivery of the DNA/RNA heterohairpin pair significantly suppressed tumor growth in mice. These findings establish a therapeutic strategy that converts RNase H1, traditionally regarded as a source of oligonucleotide toxicity, into a mechanism for selective anticancer activity through the intracellular assembly of long DNA/RNA heteroduplexes.
pool.authors: Kunihiko Morihiro, Naoki Harada, Shuichiro Koga, Yunsong Xu, Tamako Aiba, Akimitsu Okamoto

pool.title: Programmable and Dynamic DNA Localisation at Synthetic Cell Membranes
pool.abstract: Abstract Spatial and temporal organisation of membrane-associated components is fundamental to cellular signalling, yet remains difficult to engineer in minimal synthetic systems. In synthetic cells, DNA and RNA nanotechnology offer programmable molecular organisation at membranes, while in vitro transcription (IVT) enables gene expression-driven regulation. However, integrating these systems within cell-like compartments, such as giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs), remains challenging due to undesirable interactions between transcription machinery and nucleic acid assemblies. Here, we present a modular strategy that couples in situ RNA production to dynamic DNA localisation at GUV synthetic cell membranes. RNA strands, transcribed within GUVs, function as linkers that recruit DNA-conjugated cargo to lipid membranes, enabling programmable spatial organisation. Using this framework, we achieved reversible membrane localisation through toehold-mediated strand displacement and RNase H-mediated degradation. This work establishes a gene expression-driven platform for programmable and dynamic control of membrane-associated components in synthetic cells, providing a foundation for constructing dynamic signalling assemblies and higher-order cellular behaviours.
pool.authors: Chelsea Dack, Bingkun Li, Charlie Newell, Michael J. Booth

pool.title: Mapping biomedical hydrogel microspheres through scientometric and topic modeling analysis of emerging nano-enabled design strategies
pool.abstract: Hydrogel microspheres (HMs) are injectable microscale hydrogel platforms formed from crosslinked polymeric networks, with tunable porosity, stiffness, degradation behavior, surface chemistry, and cargo-loading capacity. Recent advances have expanded HMs beyond conventional controlled-release carriers into multifunctional biomedical platforms incorporating micro/nano-architectural designs, nanocomposite components, and biofunctional interfaces. However, the field-level evolution of biomedical HMs, including emerging nano-enabled design strategies, application landscapes, and validation requirements, remains insufficiently characterized. Here, we analyzed 4,399 English-language publications on biomedical HMs from the Web of Science Core Collection and PubMed between 2000 and 2025. Bibliometric mapping, co-citation analysis, keyword evolution analysis, disease/application-landscape mapping, and latent Dirichlet allocation topic modeling were integrated to identify publication growth, collaboration structures, intellectual bases, latent topics, and emerging material trends. The results show that controlled release and drug delivery remain foundational themes, whereas recent attention has increasingly focused on engineered HM platforms incorporating micro/nano-architectural features for wound healing, tissue engineering/cell delivery, bone regeneration, osteoarthritis/cartilage repair, and intervertebral disc degeneration. This study provides a data-driven map linking HM fabrication strategies, emerging micro/nano-architectural design approaches, material properties, biomedical functions, and translational validation requirements.Clinical Trial Number: Not applicable.
pool.authors: Siyang Cao, Deren Lan, Yihao Wei, Qiuyu He, Ruijie Chen, Guoqing Li, Mengjie Dong, 赵永生, Hua Zhang

pool.title: Correlating Synthesis Conditions with Structural Evolution and Near-Infrared Emission in Glutathione-Capped Gold Nanoclusters
pool.abstract: Abstract Fluorescence imaging in the near-infrared (NIR) region has attracted increasing attention in biomedical research owing to its deep tissue penetration, reduced autofluorescence, and improved imaging contrast compared with visible-light imaging. Among NIR fluorescent probes, gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) are particularly attractive because of their size-dependent emission, excellent photostability, biocompatibility, and versatile surface chemistry. Here, we systematically investigate how reaction pH, HAuCl4 concentration, and temperature influence the optical properties and structural evolution of glutathione-capped gold nanoclusters (GSH-AuNCs). The combined modulation of these parameters enables fine control over the emission characteristics, driving a transition from visible to NIR fluorescence. Near-neutral pH, elevated HAuCl4 concentration, and higher reaction temperatures promoted the formation of NIR-emissive clusters. Under optimal conditions (95 °C, C(Au) = 26 mM, and 80 μL of 1 M NaOH), GSH-AuNCs exhibited a single emission peak centered at 825 nm under 365 nm excitation, with a fluorescence intensity approximately 7.2-fold higher than that of conventional 640 nm-emissive GSH-AuNCs after absorption correction. Time-resolved fluorescence measurements revealed differences in excited-state dynamics among the differently emissive GSH-AuNCs, while circular dichroism spectroscopy showed systematic changes in ligand–metal coordination and Au(I)-thiolate shell organization accompanying the emission red shift. Zeta potential and density measurements indicated precursor concentration-dependent changes in surface charge and structural compactness, suggesting that metal core growth and ligand-shell reorganization evolve in a partially decoupled manner. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed similar elemental compositions and gold oxidation states across the differently emissive GSH-AuNCs, whereas increased Au/S ratios together with larger particle sizes determined by small-angle X-ray scattering evidenced progressive gold core growth with increasing precursor concentration. These complementary results show that the transition from red to NIR emission arises from the coupled evolution of gold core nuclearity, ligand-shell organization, and metal–ligand electronic interactions. To demonstrate biomedical applicability, GSH-AuNCs were functionalized with the SYL3C aptamer for selective detection of EpCAM-expressing PC3 cancer cells. Flow cytometry confirmed selective cellular recognition, highlighting the potential of these NIR nanoprobes for targeted cancer imaging. Overall, these findings provide a framework for engineering GSH-AuNCs with tailored structural and photophysical properties for biomedical imaging, biosensing, and image-guided therapeutic applications.
pool.authors: Bowen Wang, N. Laurand, Barbara Jachimska, Sanjay Sandhu, Daniel Doveiko, Amrutha Sankar, Christopher Kelly, Aruna Ivaturi, Yu Chen

pool.title: Cell‐Based Micro/Nanorobots: From Living Carriers to Living Therapeutic Specialists
pool.abstract: ABSTRACT Cell‐based micro/nanorobots (CMNRs) integrate intrinsic biological functions with engineered capabilities, constituting an emerging class of biohybrid robotic platforms. Unlike fully synthetic micro/nanorobots, whose functions depend entirely on artificial materials, CMNRs are constructed from living cells or cell‐derived components and can exploit unique biological capabilities. Over the past decade, CMNR research has progressed from the development of simple delivery carriers toward therapeutic specialists capable of performing diagnostic and therapeutic tasks within distinct organs. Although the complex and highly heterogeneous physiological environments of different organs impose formidable barriers, CMNRs possess intrinsic organ‐specific compatibility shaped by evolution, offering a promising strategy for improving their performance in specialized medical tasks. Here, we propose a novel framework for constructing organ‐specific therapeutic platforms. Guided by this framework, we systematically review and critically assess the biological properties, robotic functions, and recent in vivo applications of CMNRs. Despite substantial progress, a considerable gap remains between laboratory prototypes and clinical translation. This Review identifies key translational barriers that must be addressed to ensure the safety, controllability, and functional reliability of CMNRs in clinical use. Overall, a future trajectory toward organ‐specific theranostic systems is outlined to provide a conceptual basis for the clinical development of next‐generation CMNRs.
pool.authors: Junfeng Wu, Zhaoyu Zhang, Ke Xu, Enkuo Li, Yuting Cui, Yuting Zhou, Huanyu Zhou, Beipei Zhang, Shuai Jiang, Xiaodong Wang, Jialin Jiang, Lianqing Liu, Niandong Jiao

pool.title: An ATP7A‐Mediated Endogenous Regulation Bio‐Clay Enzyme Enables Self‐Amplified Copper Accumulation for Immunogenic Pyrop
pool.abstract: Tumor cells maintain abnormal metabolism to support their rapid proliferation, which often compromises the therapeutic outcomes, including pyroptosis. Inhibiting the copper transporter ATPase (ATP7A) effectively disrupts this metabolic balance, yet current exogenous ATP7A inhibition strategies suffer from poor delivery efficiency and low tumor selectivity. Herein, we developed an endogenous regulation strategy to downregulate ATP7A levels using a self-amplifying bio-clay enzyme (Bio-Clayzyme), cupriferous Prussian blue/montmorillonite (CuPB/Mt). Upon tumor cell internalization, CuPB/Mt induces a robust reactive oxygen species (ROS) storm, accompanied by antioxidant depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) exhaustion. These metabolic disturbances are associated with reduced ATP7A expression, which may subsequently impair ATP7A-mediated copper efflux. The resulting intracellular copper accumulation may further promote ROS amplification, supporting a positive feedback loop among ROS production, ATP7A downregulation, and copper retention. Specifically, the introduction of Mt optimizes the Cu d-band center and strengthens tumor cell adhesion, thereby boosting the multi-enzyme-like catalytic activity and enabling efficient utilization of short-lived ROS. Consequently, CuPB/Mt activates nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3)-dependent pyroptosis and elicits a potent anti-tumor immune response, offering an ATP7A-mediated endogenous regulatory paradigm for self-amplified catalytic therapy and immunogenic pyroptosis.

pool.title: Sigma-1 receptor activation mediates a faster antidepressant-like effect through disinhibition of the DRN5-HT-mPFCpyr neural circuit via S1R/5-HT1AR heterocomplex.
pool.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Sigma-1 receptor (S1R) represents a promising target for faster-onset antidepressants. Nevertheless, the mechanism underlying the delayed onset of therapeutic action exhibited by S1R-activating selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) remains unclear. Thus, elucidating the role of S1R in mediating faster antidepressant-like effects is of considerable significance. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to elucidate the role of S1R in mediating faster onset antidepressant-like effects and to investigate the underlying mechanism. METHODS: To detect the formation of S1R/5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 1A (5-HT1AR) heterocomplexes, in situ proximity ligation assay, co-immunoprecipitation, and co-localization techniques were employed. The functional role of these heterocomplexes was assessed through pharmacological interventions and behavioral tests. Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying their faster antidepressant-like effects were investigated using electrophysiological recordings and chemogenetic approaches. RESULTS: We provide evidence for the existence of S1R/5-HT1AR heterocomplexes in the mouse brain through in-situ PLA and co-immunoprecipitation, and by co-localization assays in primary cortical neurons, and further reveal that these heterocomplexes are predominantly localized in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN). Pharmacological activation of S1R promoted 5‑HT1AR trafficking to the plasma membrane and enhanced functional heterocomplex formation. CREB luciferase reporter assays revealed that S1R/5‑HT1AR heterocomplexes suppress 8‑OH‑DPAT-induced inhibition of forskolin-induced CREB signaling in cells co‑expressing both receptors. Electrophysiological recordings indicated that the heterocomplex attenuated the ability of 5‑HT1AR to open G protein‑gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels, thus preventing excessive neuronal hyperpolarization and promoting neuronal activity. Disrupting S1R/5‑HT1AR complexes in DRN induced depressive‑like behaviors in mice, whereas specific activation of the DRN 5-HTergic to medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) pyramidal (DRN5-HT-mPFCpyr) neuronal circuit alleviated these behavioral deficits. CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate that S1R/5-HT1AR heterocomplex activity mediates disinhibition within the DRN5-HT-mPFCpyr neuronal circuit, underpinning the rapid antidepressant-like effects elicited by S1R activation. This highlights S1R as a promising therapeutic target for the development of faster-onset antidepressants.
pool.authors: Ren P, Wang JY, Yan JZ, Chen HL, Duan JY, Xu MJ, Cui LY, Zhang LM, Li YF

pool.title: Optimization of lipid nanoparticles reduces hepatic accumulation and enhances local delivery of mRNA.
pool.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most widely used non-viral gene delivery system, particularly for mRNA therapeutics. However, predominant hepatic accumulation and poor local delivery remain major barriers to their broader application. To address this challenge, we employed a design of experiments (DOE) strategy to systematically refine LNP composition and identified an optimized formulation, SM102M. Compared with the parental SM102 formulation, SM102M markedly reduced liver-associated signal after both intramuscular and intravenous administration, while preserving or enhancing local expression after local delivery. Across multiple local administration routes, including intramuscular, intracerebroventricular, and intravitreal injection, SM102M supported localized gene delivery and gene editing with minimal liver-associated signal. Mechanistically, the altered biodistribution of SM102M was associated with reduced apolipoprotein E (ApoE) binding, lower systemic exposure, and diminished lysosomal escape in hepatocytes. SM102M also showed favorable tolerability and maintained local delivery performance under repeated administration. Together, these findings establish DOE as a practical framework for rational LNP engineering and identify a formulation with reduced hepatic reporter expression and improved local delivery performance.
pool.authors: Ma Y, Han Y, Zhou J, Xiao Y, Liu J, Sun W, Yang H, Hu G, Li S, Ji W, Guo W, Zhang L, Chen Y

pool.title: Exosomes as next-generation drug carriers: Transforming cancer therapy.
pool.abstract: Cancer remains a major global health challenge, with its growing incidence highlighting the critical need for effective and accessible treatments. Current therapeutic approaches, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, hormone therapy, and immuno-therapy, are often limited by toxicity, poor targeting, and suboptimal efficacy. These challenges have driven the development of nanotechnology-based strategies aimed at improving tumor selectivity and therapeutic outcomes. Among the most promising are extracellular vesicles, particularly exosomes (30-150 nm), which have garnered significant attention as natural nanocarriers due to their inherent role in intercellular communication and their capacity to encapsulate proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids. Exosomes can be obtained from a wide range of sources, including biological fluids, cell cultures, and unconventional origins such as plants and microorganisms. Of particular interest, milk- and colostrum-derived exosomes, particularly those of bovine origin, have emerged as a promising delivery platform owing to their scalability, biocompatibility, cost-effectiveness and suitability for oral administration. These vesicles possess immunomodulatory properties, demonstrate stability under gastrointestinal conditions, and are readily internalized by intestinal epithelial cells. Furthermore, surface engineering with targeting ligands such as folic acid can enhance tumor specific delivery by exploiting receptor overexpression while minimizing systemic toxicity. This review critically examines exosome sources, isolation and characterization methodologies, cargo-loading strategies, biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, and engineering approaches together with their applications in delivering small-molecule drugs and nucleic acid-based therapeutics to overcome multidrug resistance in cancer. In addition, current challenges related to exosome heterogeneity, manufacturing, quality control, clinical translation, and regulatory considerations are discussed, together with future perspectives for the development of exosome-based therapeutics.
pool.authors: Arif Y, Moholkar DN, Kandimalla R, Aqil F, Gupta RC

pool.title: Drug-likeness defects drive carrier-free cyanine-PROTAC self-assembly for tumor-specific protein degradation.
pool.abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) offer a powerful strategy for targeted protein degradation but suffer from poor solubility, bioavailability, and in vivo distribution due to their "beyond rule-of-five" physicochemical properties, severely limiting clinical translation. Here, we transform these intrinsic drug-likeness liabilities into a driving force for molecular self-assembly by developing a carrier-free nanoplatform in which PROTACs spontaneously co-assemble with cyanine dyes, including IR783 and the clinically approved indocyanine green (ICG). This strategy generates stable supramolecular assemblies with ultra-high PROTAC loading (up to 70 wt%) without the need for exogenous carriers, while imparting intrinsic NIR fluorescence for real-time, non-invasive in vivo tracking. The assemblies undergo stimuli-responsive disassembly upon ultrasound or X-ray irradiation, enabling spatiotemporally controlled PROTAC release within tumors. Incorporation of diselenide-bridged cyanine derivatives further confers radiosensitization capability, allowing synergistic combination with radiotherapy. In vivo studies demonstrate efficient tumor accumulation, robust target protein degradation, and potent antitumor efficacy. Collectively, this work establishes a versatile supramolecular strategy that directly addresses the long-standing delivery challenges of PROTACs and advances precise, controllable oncological therapy.
pool.authors: Pan Z, Lin T, Ullah I, Chu C, Yang W, Guo Y, El-Khouly ME, Zhang Z, Wang J, Yuan Y

pool.title: Cleavage-gated Cas13-to-DNA nanostructure transduction for target-preamplification-free viral RNA detection.
pool.abstract: CRISPR-Cas13a enables programmable RNA recognition without target nucleic-acid preamplification, but conventional assays encode collateral RNase activity by cleaving fluorescent reporters. Here, we developed a cleavage-gated strategy that converts transient Cas13a cleavage into a sequence-defined, strand-displacement-competent DNA actuator, shifting signal encoding from cumulative reporter intensity to a discrete scaffold topology. A chimeric masking hairpin (CMH) links Cas13a to a DNA nanostructure sensor (DNA-NS) by using a cleavable RNA loop to constrain a DNA-key bearing a pre-exposed toehold. Target-activated Cas13a cleaves the loop, converting the partially masked key into a strand-displacement-competent intermediate that reconfigures an M13mp18 scaffold from a linear to a looped state, producing a distinct electrophoretic mobility signature. Screening of 40 CMH-sensor-handle combinations identified a 4-nt toehold paired with an 18-nt sensor handle as the best-performing configuration within the tested design space (component-level ΔΔG = -1.19 kcal/mol at 37 °C). Using pooled crRNAs targeting the S, M, and L genomic segments of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV), the assay detected the lowest tested input concentration of 10.38 fM in all three replicates. In a retrospective case-control evaluation of 87 plasma-derived RNA samples, the assay agreed with RT-qPCR for 45 of 47 positive specimens and 40 healthy controls, yielding a positive percent agreement of 95.7% and a negative percent agreement of 100%. Replacing the crRNAs redirected recognition to Hantaan virus reference RNA without redesigning the CMH or DNA-NS. This work establishes a modular framework for topology-resolved viral RNA detection without target preamplification.
pool.authors: Lee EY, Lee DG, Kwon JS, Kim SH, Shin Y

pool.title: Computational Strategies for Investigating Phytochemicals in Drug-resistant Tuberculosis.
pool.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Tuberculosis (TB) is a serious global health concern precipitated by the pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The manifestation of drug-resistant forms of tuberculosis, such as extensively drug-resistant (XDR) and multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains, makes treatment more difficult. METHODS: Innovative methods are required to find novel therapies because traditional drug development procedures are expensive and time-consuming. So, computational phytochemistry, which utilizes computer-aided techniques to create and find novel medications from natural plant molecules, provides new opportunities for the discovery of antitubercular agents. (DR-TB). This review aims to critically evaluate the potential of computational phytochemistry in accelerating the discovery of phytochemical-based therapeutics against drug-resistant tuberculosis. Relevant literature was examined, focusing on computational approaches including molecular docking, virtual screening, quantitative structure- activity relationship (QSAR) analysis, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, artificial intelligence- assisted screening, pharmacophore modeling, and ADMET prediction for identifying promising anti-TB phytochemicals targeting key Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins. RESULTS: The reviewed studies revealed that several classes of phytochemicals, including flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and phenolic compounds, demonstrated strong binding affinities toward validated drug-resistant TB targets such as InhA, DprE1, KasA, PknB, and DNA gyrase. Studies employing integrated computational workflows combining molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and ADMET analyses provided more reliable predictions than docking-only approaches, facilitating the identification and optimization of potential anti-TB lead compounds. DISCUSSION: Given the prevalence of DR-TB and the shortcomings of existing treatments, this strategy tackles the urgent need for novel treatments. By fusing the enormous diversity of plant chemicals with computational capacity, this research offers a viable path for the revelation and development of unprecedented natural product-based anti-TB medications. CONCLUSION: Computational phytochemistry represents a promising and cost-effective strategy for prioritizing phytochemicals against MDR/XDR-TB. These encouraging in silico findings must be translated into successful treatments for drug-resistant tuberculosis, which will require more in vitro antimycobacterial screening, target-based biochemical assays, pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies, in vivo efficacy evaluation in tuberculosis models, and ultimately clinical validation. Future studies should also integrate artificial intelligence- driven drug discovery and multi-target screening approaches to improve hit identification and lead optimization for combating drug-resistant tuberculosis.
pool.authors: Sahu DR, Sahoo BM, Nanda A, Jena J, Dinda SC, Singh B, Sharma S, Agrawal A
